projectTitle: Oakmere Credit Union: The Alert That Should Have Fired
projectTagline: A 20-video, start-to-finish security-engineering build for a regional credit union -- real Sentinel detection engineering, Conditional Access hardening, and zero-trust segmentation taken from a regulatory exam finding through a genuine 36-hour detection gap that a phished service account slipped through.
businessContext: Oakmere Credit Union is a mid-size regional credit union whose regulatory examination returned three findings: insufficient detection coverage, no documented incident-response process, and legacy service accounts bypassing MFA with no documented control. Renata Ibarra, SOC Analyst, leads the remediation -- Sentinel/Defender XDR detection, Conditional Access hardening, and a zero-trust pilot -- across tenant oakmere-cu. Mid-build, a phished service account slips past a documented exclusion and goes undetected for 36 hours.
architectureSummary: The target architecture centers on Microsoft Sentinel (workspace law-oakmere-soc) and Defender XDR, Entra Conditional Access (CA-RequireMFA-AllUsers) governing a dual-cloud (Azure/AWS) identity footprint, zero-trust network micro-segmentation containing lateral movement, and independent Python automation (ip-reputation-enrichment.py) enriching sign-in telemetry against threat intelligence.

lessons.title: The Regulatory Exam Findings No One Wants to Own
lessons.summary: A routine NCUA examination flags Oakmere Credit Union's SOC for weak detection coverage, no formal incident-response process, and legacy service accounts that bypass MFA -- the discovery meeting where Renata Ibarra learns exactly what has to change before any Sentinel rule or Conditional Access policy gets built.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Over the next 20 videos you'll walk through one complete, start-to-finish security-engineering build for a fictional regional financial institution, **Oakmere Credit Union** -- a mid-size credit union with a real Microsoft Entra tenant (`oakmere-cu`) and a real Microsoft Sentinel workspace (`law-oakmere-soc`) already collecting logs, but with almost nothing tuned, documented, or enforced consistently across it. The problem isn't that Oakmere has no security tooling. It's that the tooling was turned on and left alone: default analytics rules nobody tuned, no written incident-response process, and legacy service accounts quietly excluded from multifactor authentication because turning MFA on for them once broke something and nobody ever went back to fix it properly.

You are **Renata Ibarra**, a SOC Analyst at Oakmere. This video starts exactly where a project like this has to start: a regulatory examination report lands on your VP's desk, and before a single Sentinel analytics rule gets rewritten or a single Conditional Access policy gets touched, someone has to sit down with the people who read that report line by line and understand precisely what it says, in their words, not a cleaned-up summary. By the end of this series, Oakmere has real Sentinel detection engineering, consolidated Azure and AWS identity, a Conditional Access and zero-trust pilot, and Python-based security automation -- and all of it gets tested for real by an incident that finds out exactly how much of it actually works. None of that gets designed until this meeting happens.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine your school has a hallway with security cameras and a check-in desk at the front door. An inspector comes through once a year to make sure the school is actually safe, not just pretending to be. This year the inspector writes three things in their report: some of the cameras are pointed at empty walls instead of the doors that matter, nobody has a written plan for what to do if someone sneaks in, and there's a side door that some delivery workers use every day without ever showing their badge, because showing a badge there used to jam the lock.

That's Oakmere Credit Union's security team right now. The inspector is a government examiner who checks on credit unions. Renata's job starts with sitting down with the people who read that report and asking exactly what they mean by each finding -- before anyone tries to fix the cameras, write the plan, or fix that side door.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The detail that matters in this discovery meeting isn't the headline -- 'the exam found gaps' -- it's the specific, literal wording of each finding, because that wording is what Renata will be measured against for the rest of this project. Oakmere Credit Union is examined periodically under NCUA safety-and-soundness and information-security guidance, consistent with FFIEC expectations most financial institutions operate under. This cycle's report names three findings, and each one maps to a real, specific gap in how Oakmere's environment is actually configured today.

**Weak detection coverage** means Microsoft Sentinel is deployed -- the workspace `law-oakmere-soc` has been collecting sign-in and endpoint telemetry for months -- but almost every enabled analytics rule is an unmodified Microsoft out-of-the-box template, never tuned against Oakmere's actual user population, and there is no documented mapping of which real attack techniques those rules would and would not catch. **No formal incident-response process** means there is no written IR plan: no defined severity levels, no named on-call roles, no runbook for who does what when an alert actually fires. And **legacy service accounts that bypass MFA** is the finding Renata should treat as the most urgent, because it's the one tied to standing, provable risk rather than a documentation gap: a handful of old automation and integration accounts were excluded from multifactor authentication at some point in the past -- a common, defensible short-term move when a legacy system couldn't handle an MFA challenge -- and that exclusion was never revisited.

**Denise Okafor**, Oakmere's VP of Information Security, sponsors this project and is the person whose name is actually on the response the examiner expects back. **Thomas Reyes**, Director of IT Infrastructure, owns the Entra tenant `oakmere-cu` itself -- the actual identity configuration, including whichever service accounts currently sit outside MFA enforcement. **Priya Nair**, Compliance & Risk Officer, owns the regulatory relationship and is the one who can tell Renata exactly what the examiner wrote versus what later got summarized into a two-line action item. Getting the literal finding language from Priya, and the literal current-state configuration from Thomas, before drafting a single requirement, is what keeps the rest of this project honest about what's actually broken.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Walk in already knowing what you don't know

Before the meeting, write down what you need to confirm, not just what you expect to hear:

- What is the exact wording of each of the three examiner findings, and which systems does each one actually point at?
- How many service accounts are currently excluded from MFA, and does anyone have a complete list?
- Is there any written incident-response documentation at all today, even an outdated one?

## Step 2 -- Run the meeting and get the findings in Priya's own words

```
PRIYA:    The exam report has three findings this cycle, and I want you to
          hear the literal language, not my summary. First: "detection
          coverage across privileged and remote access scenarios is
          insufficient to reliably identify unauthorized access." Second:
          "the credit union lacks a documented, tested incident response
          plan." Third -- and this is the one that worries me most --
          "certain service accounts are configured to bypass multifactor
          authentication requirements without a documented compensating
          control."

RENATA:   On that third one -- do we know how many accounts, and why they're
          excluded?

PRIYA:    Not precisely, no. That's part of why I need you and Thomas
          involved. I know it's more than one. I don't have a verified
          count or a documented reason beyond "it broke something once."
```

## Step 3 -- Ask Thomas Reyes what the identity environment actually looks like today

```
RENATA:   Thomas, walk me through the MFA exclusion. What's actually
          configured in oakmere-cu right now?

THOMAS:   We have a Conditional Access setup, but it's not consistent.
          Human users are mostly covered. A handful of legacy service
          accounts -- the ones tied to older integrations, things like
          core-banking sync jobs -- got carved out of MFA enforcement a
          while back because the challenge broke the automated sign-in
          flow. Nobody circled back to fix that properly with a real
          non-interactive auth method. They're just... excluded.

RENATA:   Is there a documented list of exactly which accounts, and is
          there any other control watching what those accounts actually
          do once they're signed in?

THOMAS:   Not a clean one, no. That's a real gap, and it's the one I'm
          least comfortable with out of all three findings.
```

## Step 4 -- Ask Denise Okafor what "fixed" has to mean

```
RENATA:    Denise, before I draft anything -- what does the examiner, and
           the board, actually need to see to consider this closed?

DENISE:    Three things, matching the three findings. Real, tuned
           detection -- not default rules nobody's looked at. A written,
           tested incident-response process with actual roles and
           runbooks. And a documented, risk-reduced answer for those
           service accounts -- either real MFA-equivalent controls or a
           compensating control we can defend to an examiner with a
           straight face. I don't want cosmetic fixes. I want this team
           able to say, truthfully, exactly what we can detect and exactly
           what we can't yet.
```

## Step 5 -- Confirm Oakmere's current environment, in writing

```
OAKMERE CREDIT UNION -- CURRENT STATE (AS OF THIS EXAM CYCLE)

Entra tenant:        oakmere-cu
Sentinel workspace:  law-oakmere-soc (collecting sign-in + endpoint
                     telemetry; analytics rules largely unmodified
                     Microsoft templates)
Incident response:   No current documented IR plan, severity model, or
                     on-call runbook
MFA coverage:        Human users mostly enforced; an unconfirmed number
                     of legacy service accounts excluded, no documented
                     compensating control
```

## Step 6 -- Write the discovery summary and confirm it with Denise

```
OAKMERE CREDIT UNION -- DISCOVERY SUMMARY

Business problem:   A regulatory examination found three gaps: weak
                    detection coverage, no formal incident-response
                    process, and legacy service accounts bypassing MFA
                    without a documented compensating control.
Sponsor:            Denise Okafor, VP of Information Security.
Key roles:          Thomas Reyes (Director of IT Infrastructure, owns
                    the oakmere-cu tenant and its Conditional Access
                    configuration), Priya Nair (Compliance & Risk
                    Officer, owns the regulatory relationship and the
                    literal exam language).
Environment:        Entra tenant oakmere-cu; Sentinel workspace
                    law-oakmere-soc.
```

Send this summary to Denise Okafor and ask directly: "Did I capture this accurately?" Every requirement written in the next lesson traces back to a line in this document -- and her sign-off on the real finding language is what keeps this project honest about what Oakmere actually needs to fix, not what sounds good in a slide.

lessons.title: Scoping the SOC Modernization and Zero-Trust Pilot
lessons.summary: Drawing a hard line around what this project actually ships -- real Sentinel/Defender XDR detection engineering, Azure and AWS identity consolidation, a scoped Conditional Access and zero-trust pilot, and Python-based security automation -- and naming what's explicitly deferred, including a full enterprise-wide zero-trust rollout.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
The discovery meeting gave Renata three honest findings and a sponsor who wants real fixes, not cosmetic ones. This lesson turns that into a written scope: exactly what this project builds, and just as importantly, what it explicitly does not. V1 of Oakmere's SOC modernization ships four things: tuned Sentinel detection engineering and Defender XDR coverage in the `law-oakmere-soc` workspace; consolidated identity visibility across Oakmere's Azure (`oakmere-cu`) and AWS footprints; a Conditional Access policy, `CA-RequireMFA-AllUsers`, enforcing MFA tenant-wide with one explicit, documented exclusion group, `CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt`, as a zero-trust pilot; and Python-based security automation, starting with a daily threat-intel enrichment job, run as a scheduled Azure Automation runbook.

What's explicitly out of scope, named in writing rather than left to assumption, is a full enterprise-wide zero-trust rollout -- this project pilots the pattern on a deliberately narrow, high-risk population (legacy service accounts) rather than attempting every identity in the tenant at once. It does not replace Oakmere's core banking platform or redesign how any legacy integration authenticates at the application layer -- Thomas Reyes's team keeps owning that. And it does not stand up a brand-new SOAR or ticketing platform -- the Python automation this project builds integrates with what Oakmere already has, rather than replacing it.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine the school from the last lesson agrees to fix what the inspector found. 'Make it safer' doesn't tell the custodian what to actually do, so they get specific: point the cameras at the real doors, write down exactly what to do if someone sneaks in, and for that one side door the delivery workers use, test a new badge reader on just that door first instead of ripping out every door's lock in the building on day one.

That's the plan for Oakmere. The team fixes the security cameras (Sentinel detection), writes the emergency plan (incident response), and tests a new, stricter badge-check on the one risky side door -- the handful of legacy accounts -- before trying to change every lock in the building at once. They also build a little automated helper that checks a daily list of known troublemakers against who's come through the door. What they don't do yet: rebuild the whole bank's core system, or throw out all their existing tools for brand-new ones.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Scope discipline matters here because 'fix the exam findings' is exactly the kind of mandate that invites scope creep the moment real budget and executive attention exist behind it. It would be easy for this project to balloon into 'redesign every identity in the tenant' or 'replace the core banking integration layer' -- neither belongs in V1.

The Conditional Access and zero-trust pilot is deliberately scoped narrow and named precisely: `CA-RequireMFA-AllUsers` becomes the tenant-wide MFA policy, with exactly one exclusion group, `CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt`, holding the legacy and break-glass service accounts that can't yet take an interactive MFA challenge. This is a real, common temporary migration practice -- but this project commits to tracking that exclusion group as a named, monitored risk rather than a quiet default, which is the gap the examiner actually flagged. A full zero-trust rollout across every human and non-human identity at Oakmere is explicitly deferred as a future phase; this project proves the pattern works on the highest-risk, smallest population first.

Detection engineering work stays inside Sentinel and Defender XDR against `law-oakmere-soc` -- tuning and building real analytics rules, not replacing the SIEM. Identity consolidation covers visibility across Azure and AWS so Renata's team can correlate sign-in activity across both clouds, but it does not mean migrating AWS IAM into Entra or vice versa. Python automation starts with one real, running capability -- a daily IP-reputation enrichment job against sign-in logs -- deliberately scoped small enough to actually finish and prove the automation pattern, rather than a sprawling SOAR platform that risks never shipping. Each of these choices traces back to a finding from the discovery meeting; none of them is a default template someone copied in.

lessons.title: Setting Real Targets: MTTD, MTTR, and Detection Coverage
lessons.summary: Turning 'better detection' into measurable success criteria -- a 4-hour MTTD target for high-severity identity alerts, an 8-hour MTTR target for containment, documented analytics-rule coverage for the identity techniques that matter most, and a 24-hour freshness target for the Python threat-intel runbook -- plus the honest scenario that stress-tests every one of them.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Scope is locked, but 'better detection' and 'a written IR process' aren't success criteria yet -- they're intentions. This lesson turns them into numbers Renata can actually be held to, and that this series can honestly check later. Four targets get fixed here. **Mean time to detect (MTTD):** high-severity identity-based alerts -- sign-ins that should trigger a Sentinel analytics rule -- get surfaced within 4 hours of occurring. **Mean time to respond (MTTR):** once a high-severity incident is confirmed, containment action starts within 8 hours. **Detection coverage:** every analytics rule in `law-oakmere-soc` is mapped in writing to the specific sign-in scenario it's meant to catch, including exactly how it treats accounts in `CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt` -- no rule ships without someone being able to say, in plain language, what it does and does not cover. **Automation freshness:** the Python threat-intel enrichment runbook flags a known-malicious IP match within 24 hours of that IP appearing in the feed.

This lesson also runs one honest sanity check against all four targets at once, using the exact kind of account this project is piloting new controls on: a legacy service account, excluded from MFA by `CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt` and tagged `ServiceAccount` for noise reduction, that has a rare but real interactive sign-in from an unexpected country. Whether Sentinel, the Conditional Access pilot, and the Python automation actually catch that scenario within these targets is not assumed here -- it's exactly what later lessons in this series have to prove, honestly, once the detection architecture and the automation actually exist.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine the school decides 'catch problems faster' isn't good enough -- they need a real number. So they agree: if something serious happens at the side door, someone has to notice within half a school day, and once they notice, someone has to actually go deal with it within a full school day. They also agree to write down, for every camera, exactly what it's supposed to catch -- including one tricky camera that's told to ignore the delivery workers' badge swipes so it doesn't cry wolf every single day.

Then they ask themselves a hard question: what if one of those delivery workers' badges gets stolen, and the thief uses it to walk in the front door instead of the side door, on a day they don't normally work? Would the camera that's told to ignore delivery workers still catch that? That's the exact kind of question Renata has to ask about Oakmere's own service accounts before trusting the numbers on paper.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A target that can't be tested is a hope, not a requirement -- so each of the four numbers here is written specifically to be checkable against real telemetry once the detection architecture exists, not just plausible on a slide.

The MTTD and MTTR targets -- 4 hours to detect a high-severity identity alert, 8 hours to begin containment once confirmed -- come directly from Denise Okafor's standard: the board and the examiner both need a number, not a sentiment, and these two match what FFIEC-aligned peer institutions typically commit to for identity-based incidents at Oakmere's size. The detection-coverage target is the one that does the most real work: every analytics rule in `law-oakmere-soc` must have a written statement of exactly what it covers and what it deliberately excludes. This matters because the examiner's finding wasn't just 'not enough rules' -- it was that nobody could say with confidence what the existing rules actually caught. A rule that excludes a category of accounts for a defensible reason, like cutting noise from legitimate automated multi-region activity, is not itself a problem; an *undocumented* exclusion that nobody can name is the problem, and that distinction is the whole point of this target.

The automation-freshness target -- a known-malicious IP match surfaced within 24 hours -- is deliberately set as a real, named number for the Python runbook this project builds, not an open-ended 'as soon as possible.' It is also deliberately the softest of the four targets, because daily-batch threat-intel enrichment is a real, common pattern with a real latency cost, and this project is honest about that cost up front rather than overselling the automation as near-real-time.

The sanity-check scenario -- a legacy service account, exempted from MFA by `CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt` and tagged `ServiceAccount` for detection-rule noise reduction, producing a rare but real interactive sign-in from an unexpected country -- is run deliberately now, before any rule is built, because it's precisely the kind of edge case that two independently reasonable scoping decisions (an MFA exemption for automation, and a noise-reduction exclusion for detection) can combine to miss entirely. Flagging that risk here, in writing, with Denise, Thomas, and Priya, is what keeps the later architecture decision honest about a tradeoff it is choosing to accept for now rather than one it accidentally overlooked.

RENATA:   'Better detection' and 'faster response' aren't things I can
          actually check later. What number would satisfy you and the
          board?

DENISE:   For a high-severity identity alert -- someone who shouldn't be
          signing in, signing in -- I want to know within 4 hours. And
          once we've confirmed it's real, I want containment action
          started within 8 hours. Those are the two numbers I need to be
          able to say out loud to an examiner.
```

MTTD-1: High-severity identity-based alerts (interactive sign-ins that
        should trigger a Sentinel analytics rule) are surfaced within 4
        hours of occurring.
MTTR-1: Once a high-severity incident is confirmed, containment action
        begins within 8 hours.
```

          something specific, not a vague percentage.

RENATA:   Agreed. Every analytics rule in law-oakmere-soc gets a one-line

          and anything it deliberately excludes -- including exactly how

          ships without that sentence existing somewhere Denise and Priya

```

       Denise Okafor.
```

## Step 4 -- Fix the automation-freshness target

```
RENATA:   The Python threat-intel enrichment job is a daily batch run,
          not real-time. I want to be upfront about that latency instead
          of promising something the automation can't actually deliver.

DENISE:   What's the real number, then?

RENATA:   A known-malicious IP match gets flagged within 24 hours of that
          IP showing up in the feed. That's honest about the batch
          cadence, and it's still a lot faster than finding out from a
          customer or an examiner.
```

```
TARGET -- AUTOMATION FRESHNESS

AUTO-1: The daily IP-reputation enrichment runbook flags a sign-in that
        matches a known-malicious IP within 24 hours of that IP
        appearing in the threat-intel feed.
```

## Step 5 -- Stress-test all four targets against one honest scenario

```
Scenario: A legacy service account is a member of
          CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt (excluded from MFA) and is
          tagged ServiceAccount in Sentinel for detection-rule noise
          reduction. On a given day, that account authenticates
          interactively -- rare, but real -- from a country it has never
          signed in from before.

Question: Does MTTD-1 actually hold for this exact account, given that
          two separate, independently reasonable exclusions -- an MFA
          exemption and a detection-rule noise exclusion -- both apply to
          it at once?
```

Walk this scenario past Denise, Thomas, and Priya directly and ask: "Are we comfortable this is a known, accepted tradeoff for now, or does it need to be closed before this counts as done?" Write down whatever they decide -- that decision is the one later lessons in this series are going to test for real.

## Step 6 -- Get the four targets signed off

Save MTTD-1, MTTR-1, COV-1, and AUTO-1 alongside the Lesson 1 and Lesson 2 artifacts. Get explicit sign-off from Denise Okafor on all four, and flag the Step 5 scenario in writing as a named, open risk the architecture work in the next lesson has to account for -- not something to quietly assume is already handled.

lessons.title: Designing the Target Sentinel and Defender XDR Detection Architecture
lessons.summary: The first real architecture decision: which data connectors feed law-oakmere-soc, how Defender XDR unifies endpoint/identity/email signal into Sentinel incidents, and the specific analytics rule, 'Impossible Travel - Interactive Sign-ins,' scoped to exclude ServiceAccount-tagged accounts to cut automation noise -- a deliberate, documented tradeoff this series commits to testing honestly, not a default nobody looked at.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With scope and targets locked, this lesson makes the first real architecture decision: the shape of detection coverage in `law-oakmere-soc` before a single rule gets written in a later implementation lesson. Three decisions get fixed here. First, the **data connectors**: Entra ID sign-in and audit logs, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, Microsoft Defender for Identity, and Microsoft Defender for Office 365 all feed into the workspace, unified through **Microsoft Defender XDR** so an identity-based detection can be correlated against endpoint and email signal for the same user, not investigated as four disconnected alerts. Second, the **rule inventory shape**: a small set of scheduled analytics rules targeting the techniques that map to real Oakmere risk -- credential-based initial access, anomalous privileged sign-ins, and impossible-travel sign-in patterns -- each with the documented coverage statement COV-1 requires.

Third, and the decision this lesson spends the most time on: the specific design of the rule named **'Impossible Travel - Interactive Sign-ins.'** It is built to catch sign-ins from the same account in two geographically implausible locations in an implausibly short window -- but it is deliberately scoped to exclude any account tagged `ServiceAccount` in Sentinel, specifically to cut false-positive noise from legitimate automated systems that really do authenticate from multiple regions as part of normal, non-interactive operation. This lesson names that exclusion choice explicitly, in writing, as a real tradeoff with a real cost -- the Step 5 scenario from the previous lesson is exactly the cost -- and commits this series to testing honestly, later, whether that tradeoff holds up in practice. It does not yet claim it does.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you're designing a new alarm system for the school. You decide which doors get sensors, which cameras talk to which guard station, and how the guard station is supposed to connect a camera alert at the side door to a badge-swipe record from the same minute, instead of looking at them as two separate, unrelated beeps.

Then you design one specific alarm: a 'this person can't be in two places at once' alarm, for anyone who badges in at one door and then badges in at a door across campus five minutes later -- that's physically impossible, so it means something's wrong. But you decide that alarm should ignore the delivery workers' badges, because delivery trucks really do drop things at multiple doors in a short window and that used to set the alarm off constantly for no real reason. You write that decision down on purpose, because you already know it means if a delivery worker's badge gets stolen and used to walk in a door they don't normally use, this particular alarm won't catch it. You're not hiding that risk -- you're writing it down so everyone knows it's a real, chosen tradeoff, not an accident.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This architecture decision earns scrutiny specifically because its most important design choice is the one most likely to look, on the surface, like a routine noise-reduction tweak rather than a real security tradeoff.

The connector layer is straightforward: Entra ID sign-in and audit logs, Defender for Endpoint, Defender for Identity, and Defender for Office 365 all feed `law-oakmere-soc`, with Defender XDR providing the correlation layer so an incident groups related signal across identity, endpoint, and email for the same entity instead of forcing an analyst to manually stitch four separate alert queues together. This directly supports the MTTD-1 target from the previous lesson -- correlated incidents surface faster than four raw alerts an analyst has to notice are related.

The rule that deserves the most scrutiny is **'Impossible Travel - Interactive Sign-ins.'** Its core logic is a standard, well-understood detection pattern: flag the same account authenticating from two locations whose distance and elapsed time make both sign-ins implausible. The design decision layered on top is scoping it to exclude any account carrying the `ServiceAccount` tag in Sentinel. The justification is real and defensible on its own terms: legitimate automated systems -- integration jobs, sync services, monitoring agents -- genuinely do authenticate from multiple regions or data centers as part of normal, non-interactive operation, and without this exclusion the rule would generate enough false positives from that normal behavior that analysts would be trained to ignore it, which defeats the point of having it at all.

The cost of that exclusion, named explicitly here rather than discovered later, is that it excludes an account from this rule's coverage based on what the account *is* (tagged as a service account at all) rather than what kind of sign-in it's actually performing in a given moment. A service account's routine, non-interactive, automated sign-ins are exactly the behavior the exclusion is meant to quiet -- but if that same account were ever used for a genuine, rare, interactive sign-in, this scoping has no way to tell the difference, because it never looks at sign-in type or the calling application at all. A finer-grained design -- scoping the exclusion to non-interactive sign-in type plus a known automation app ID, rather than the account's tag -- would preserve the noise reduction for routine automated traffic while still catching a rare interactive sign-in on that same account. That finer-grained design is a real option Thomas Reyes and Renata discuss and consciously set aside for V1, in favor of the simpler tag-based exclusion, because the simpler version ships faster and the tag-based model is what Sentinel's entity-tagging already supports out of the box. This lesson commits that choice to writing, as the COV-1 coverage statement for this specific rule, precisely so the tradeoff identified in the Lesson 3 sanity check is traceable to a real architecture decision, made with eyes open, rather than an oversight nobody can explain later.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- List the real constraints this architecture has to satisfy

```
CONSTRAINTS FROM LESSONS 1-3:
  - MTTD-1: high-severity identity alerts surfaced within 4 hours.
  - COV-1: every analytics rule gets a documented coverage + exclusion
    statement, reviewed by Thomas, signed off by Denise.
  - The Lesson 3 sanity check: a CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt account
    tagged ServiceAccount, with a rare real interactive sign-in from an
    unexpected country, is a named open risk this architecture has to
    account for -- not assume away.
```

## Step 2 -- Fix the connector layer

```
DECISION: Feed law-oakmere-soc from four connectors, unified through
          Microsoft Defender XDR:
            - Entra ID Sign-in logs + Audit logs
            - Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
            - Microsoft Defender for Identity
            - Microsoft Defender for Office 365
WHY:      Defender XDR's correlation layer groups related identity,
          endpoint, and email signal into one incident per real entity,
          instead of four disconnected alerts an analyst has to manually
          connect -- directly supporting MTTD-1.
```

## Step 3 -- Fix the rule inventory shape

```
PLANNED ANALYTICS RULES (law-oakmere-soc), scheduled, KQL-based:
  1. Impossible Travel - Interactive Sign-ins
  2. Anomalous Sign-ins to Privileged Roles
  3. Credential-Based Initial Access Indicators
  (Each rule gets a one-sentence COV-1 statement before it ships --
   written in a later implementation lesson, not here.)
```

## Step 4 -- Design "Impossible Travel - Interactive Sign-ins" and name its tradeoff

```
RENATA:   I want to sketch this rule's scoping logic now, before anyone
          writes production KQL, because the exclusion choice is a real
          design decision, not a default.

THOMAS:   Agreed. The straightforward version excludes by account tag --
          anything tagged ServiceAccount in Sentinel is out of scope for
          this rule entirely. That's fast to build and it's what our
          entity tagging already supports.

RENATA:   And the cost of that is: if one of those tagged accounts ever
          does a real interactive sign-in -- rare, but it happens -- this
          rule has no way to tell that apart from its normal automated
          traffic, because it never looks at sign-in type or the calling
          application at all.

THOMAS:   Right. The more precise version would scope the exclusion to
          non-interactive sign-in type plus the account's known
          automation app ID instead of the tag -- that would still catch
          a rare interactive sign-in on the same account. It's more work
          to build and verify correctly.

RENATA:   Let's write down, in the coverage statement, that V1 uses the
          tag-based exclusion as a conscious tradeoff for speed, and that
          the finer-grained, sign-in-type-plus-app-ID version is the
          known next step if this rule's accepted risk ever needs
          tightening.
```

```
# Planned rule logic sketch -- law-oakmere-soc
# "Impossible Travel - Interactive Sign-ins"
# NOT final production KQL; a design-time sketch to agree the scoping
# logic before implementation.

SigninLogs
| where ResultType == 0                         // successful sign-ins
| where isnotempty(LocationDetails)
| where AccountTag != "ServiceAccount"           // <-- the exclusion
                                                  //     decision this
                                                  //     lesson names
| summarize Countries = make_set(tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion)),
            SignInCount = count()
            by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where array_length(Countries) > 1
```

```
COV-1 STATEMENT -- Impossible Travel - Interactive Sign-ins

Covers:     Successful sign-ins from the same account, from two or more
            countries, within a one-hour window.
Excludes:   Any account tagged ServiceAccount in Sentinel -- by design,
            to cut false positives from legitimate multi-region
            automated activity.
Known cost: A tagged ServiceAccount's rare, real interactive sign-in is
            not covered by this rule under the V1 (tag-based) scoping.
            A sign-in-type-plus-app-ID scoping would close this gap and
            is the identified next step if this risk needs tightening.
Reviewed:   Thomas Reyes. Signed off: Denise Okafor.
```

## Step 5 -- Confirm the architecture decision log

```
DECISION LOG -- OAKMERE DETECTION ARCHITECTURE (V1)

Workspace:        law-oakmere-soc
Connectors:       Entra ID Sign-in + Audit logs, Defender for Endpoint,
                  Defender for Identity, Defender for Office 365
Correlation:      Microsoft Defender XDR unifies connector signal into
                  incidents per entity
Planned rules:    Impossible Travel - Interactive Sign-ins; Anomalous
                  Sign-ins to Privileged Roles; Credential-Based Initial
                  Access Indicators
Named tradeoff:   Impossible Travel rule excludes by ServiceAccount tag,
                  not by sign-in type + app ID, as a conscious V1
                  scoping choice with a documented, accepted cost
```

Walk this architecture past Denise Okafor and Thomas Reyes before the identity and Conditional Access architecture lesson that follows: does the connector layer and the named tradeoff on the Impossible Travel rule still make sense against MTTD-1 and COV-1? This decision log is now fixed for the rest of this series. Whether the tag-based exclusion's accepted cost ever actually gets paid is real work this series is honestly built to test later -- not something this lesson declares safe just because the reasoning behind it is sound.

**Up next:** the identity architecture that defines `CA-RequireMFA-AllUsers` and the `CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt` exclusion group itself -- the other half of the tradeoff named in this lesson.

lessons.title: Designing Conditional Access and Consolidating Azure + AWS Identity
lessons.summary: Planning Entra ID tenant oakmere-cu's tenant-wide MFA policy and the Azure+AWS identity consolidation -- and the one named, signed-off exception for three legacy service accounts that can't yet do interactive MFA.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
The regulatory exam's finding was blunt: legacy service accounts at Oakmere Credit Union bypass MFA, and nobody had written down which ones, why, or for how long. This lesson is where Renata Ibarra plans the fix, before a single policy gets turned on. Two things get designed here. First, a tenant-wide Conditional Access policy, **CA-RequireMFA-AllUsers**, requiring multi-factor authentication for every sign-in into the **oakmere-cu** Entra ID tenant -- no app, no user, no exception, unless that exception is named in writing. Second, a plan for consolidating Oakmere's AWS IAM users into that same Entra tenant through **AWS IAM Identity Center**, so a teller-services engineer with access to both the core banking platform in Azure and reporting infrastructure in AWS has exactly one identity, one MFA posture, and one audit trail -- not two separate directories quietly drifting apart.

The part of this plan that matters most isn't the policy that requires MFA -- it's the plan for the one place it doesn't, yet. Three legacy, break-glass-style service accounts run scheduled jobs and integrations that were built years before Conditional Access existed at Oakmere, and none of them can complete an interactive MFA prompt. Rather than let that stay an unwritten gap -- which is exactly what the regulators flagged -- this lesson plans a single, scoped exclusion group, **CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt**, holding exactly those three accounts, with a written risk acceptance, an owner, a review cadence, and a committed migration path off of it. This is a real, common pattern during an MFA rollout. It is also a real, live risk, and this lesson's job is to make sure that risk is visible on paper, not discovered the hard way.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a bank building where every single employee has to badge in AND type a PIN at every door -- no exceptions, because that's the new rule after an inspector found some doors with no PIN pad at all. Then someone points out: three delivery robots that restock the back office every night physically can't type a PIN, they only have a badge reader built in. So the building manager doesn't just quietly leave those three doors unlocked and hope nobody notices. She writes it down: these exact three robots, this exact door, reviewed every three months, with an actual plan to fit them with a different kind of lock soon so this exception can go away for good.

That's what Renata plans here for Oakmere Credit Union. Almost everyone and everything now needs two real proofs of identity to get in anywhere. Three old automated accounts can't do that yet, so instead of a silent gap, there's one named list, one reason, one plan to close it -- and a second project, planned alongside it, to let people use the same single ID badge for both of Oakmere's computer systems instead of carrying two different badges that nobody's comparing against each other.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The Conditional Access policy itself is the straightforward half of this plan: **CA-RequireMFA-AllUsers** targets all users and all cloud apps in the oakmere-cu tenant, with a grant control of "Require multi-factor authentication," assigned tenant-wide with no app-specific carve-outs. That's the policy the regulatory exam should have found already in place.

The half that deserves real scrutiny is the exclusion. **CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt** is planned as a security group with a hard, named membership of exactly three accounts -- automation and integration identities that predate Conditional Access at Oakmere and that cannot complete an interactive MFA challenge today. The plan treats this group as a liability with a name and an owner, not a convenience: every account added to it is an account that, if its password alone is ever obtained, authenticates successfully with nothing else required. Three controls get written into the plan specifically because of that: a hard cap on membership enforced by change-control review (nothing gets added to this group without a documented reason), a quarterly access review co-signed by Renata and the identity team lead, and a committed migration target -- each of the three accounts moves to certificate-based authentication or a managed identity, at which point it comes out of the exclusion group and the group itself eventually has zero members.

The AWS consolidation is planned as federation, not duplication: AWS IAM Identity Center is configured with Entra ID as its external identity provider over SAML, so a sign-in to AWS is actually a sign-in to the oakmere-cu tenant wearing an AWS hat -- meaning it's subject to CA-RequireMFA-AllUsers like everything else. SCIM provisioning keeps AWS permission sets mapped to Entra security groups, so adding someone to an Entra group like `AWS-Core-Banking-ReadOnly` is what grants the matching AWS permission set, instead of a parallel IAM user with its own password that nobody is rotating or reviewing on the same schedule. The plan is explicit that this consolidation doesn't, by itself, touch the three legacy service accounts' exemption -- those accounts are an Entra-side exception regardless of which cloud they ultimately reach.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Inventory what actually bypasses MFA today

Before writing a policy, Renata and the identity team confirm exactly which accounts cannot do interactive MFA and why:

```text
LEGACY/BREAK-GLASS SERVICE ACCOUNTS -- CANNOT DO INTERACTIVE MFA

Account                      Purpose                              Owner
svc-core-banking-sync        Nightly core-banking data sync       Core Banking Eng
svc-branch-reporting-sync    Branch reporting ETL job             Data/Reporting
svc-atm-settlement-batch     Overnight ATM settlement batch       Payments Ops
```

## Step 2 -- Define the tenant-wide MFA policy

```powershell
# Conditional Access policy via Microsoft Graph PowerShell -- planned shape
$params = @{
  displayName = "CA-RequireMFA-AllUsers"
  state       = "enabled"
  conditions  = @{
    users = @{ includeUsers = @("All") }
    applications = @{ includeApplications = @("All") }
  }
  grantControls = @{
    operator        = "OR"
    builtInControls = @("mfa")
  }
}
New-MgIdentityConditionalAccessPolicy -BodyParameter $params
```

## Step 3 -- Create the named exclusion group, and nothing else

```powershell
# One group, exactly three members, no open membership rule
New-MgGroup -DisplayName "CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt" \
  -MailEnabled:$false -SecurityEnabled:$true -MailNickname "ca-legacy-svc-exempt"

# Add the three named accounts -- each addition is a change-control record
Add-MgGroupMember -GroupId $exemptGroupId -DirectoryObjectId $svcCoreBankingSyncId
Add-MgGroupMember -GroupId $exemptGroupId -DirectoryObjectId $svcBranchReportingSyncId
Add-MgGroupMember -GroupId $exemptGroupId -DirectoryObjectId $svcAtmSettlementBatchId
```

Update `CA-RequireMFA-AllUsers` to exclude this one group -- the only exclusion the policy has:

```powershell
$params.conditions.users.excludeGroups = @($exemptGroupId)
Update-MgIdentityConditionalAccessPolicy -ConditionalAccessPolicyId $caPolicyId -BodyParameter $params
```

## Step 4 -- Write the risk acceptance, out loud, before the policy goes live

```text
RISK ACCEPTANCE -- CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt

Risk:        Three service accounts authenticate with a password only,
             no MFA, because they cannot complete an interactive
             challenge with their current authentication method.
Accepted by: Renata Ibarra (SOC), [Identity Team Lead], sign-off
             required before CA-RequireMFA-AllUsers goes live.
Compensating plan: network micro-segmentation pilot (next lesson)
             restricts each account's reach to only the systems it
             actually needs, so a compromised credential here cannot
             move laterally even without MFA.
Review cadence: quarterly, co-signed by Renata and the identity team.
Migration target: each account moves to certificate-based auth or a
             managed identity; the group has zero members once that's
             done for all three.
```

## Step 5 -- Plan the AWS IAM Identity Center federation

```text
# Planned shape, not yet applied
Identity provider for AWS IAM Identity Center: Entra ID (SAML)
SCIM provisioning: enabled, Entra groups -> IAM Identity Center permission sets

Example mapping:
  Entra group "AWS-Core-Banking-ReadOnly"  -> AWS permission set "CoreBankingReadOnly"
  Entra group "AWS-Reporting-Admin"        -> AWS permission set "ReportingAdmin"
```

A sign-in to AWS now routes through Entra ID first, which means it is already subject to `CA-RequireMFA-AllUsers` -- consolidation, not a second identity system running in parallel.

## Step 6 -- Confirm with stakeholders before anything goes live

Renata walks this exact plan -- the tenant-wide policy, the three-account exclusion, the risk acceptance, and the AWS federation -- past the CISO and the core banking engineering lead, and gets written sign-off on the exclusion specifically, since that's the line most likely to quietly grow past three accounts once the policy is live and someone else hits an MFA wall.

Wrote a formal risk acceptance with quarterly review and a migration target to certificate-based auth / managed identity. Planned AWS IAM Identity Center federated to Entra via SAML with SCIM group-to-permission-set mapping, so AWS access inherits the same MFA policy.

That exception is documented, owned, and reviewed quarterly -- not a silent gap. We've also planned consolidating AWS access under the same identity system so there's one MFA posture across both clouds instead of two.

We're also merging our AWS and Azure sign-in systems into one, so our security posture is consistent no matter which cloud someone is accessing.

lessons.title: Planning the Zero-Trust Micro-Segmentation Pilot
lessons.summary: Planning a network micro-segmentation pilot that restricts Oakmere's riskiest accounts -- starting with the three MFA-exempt legacy service accounts -- to only the specific network paths they actually need.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
The last lesson named a real, accepted risk: three legacy service accounts, including **svc-core-banking-sync**, sign in with a password only, no MFA, because they can't do an interactive challenge yet. That risk acceptance leaned on one promise -- a compensating network control -- and this lesson is where that promise actually gets planned. Renata and the security engineering team design a **zero-trust micro-segmentation pilot**: instead of trusting the internal network the way a flat, perimeter-only network does, every legacy service account's reach gets restricted, by explicit policy, to only the specific destination it actually needs to talk to.

For `svc-core-banking-sync` specifically, the plan is to restrict its network path down to exactly the core-banking sync service's own endpoint -- nothing else on Oakmere's network is reachable from that account's traffic, by default. The pilot deliberately starts with the three accounts named in `CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt`, because they're the highest-risk identities in the tenant right now -- no MFA, and until this pilot ships, no network restriction either. This lesson plans the segmentation; it does not build it yet, and it's honest that this control limits *lateral movement*, not the risk of the credential itself being used at the one place it's still allowed to go.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine giving three delivery robots keycards that only ever open one specific storage room -- never the vault, never the offices, never anywhere else in the building, even if someone steals the card and tries it on every other door. That's the opposite of a master key: even in the worst case, the card only ever works in the one place it's supposed to.

That's what this lesson plans for Oakmere's riskiest automated accounts. They already don't have to prove who they are twice, which is a real risk Renata wrote down last lesson. So this lesson plans a second kind of protection that doesn't depend on the password at all: wherever those accounts are allowed to go on the network gets shrunk down to exactly one destination each. If someone ever does steal one of those passwords, they don't get the whole building -- they get one locked room, and nothing else.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The pilot is planned around two Azure network primitives working together: a **default-deny Network Security Group baseline** applied to the subnets the legacy service accounts' workloads run in, and a small number of **explicit allow rules**, one per account, scoped to the exact destination each one legitimately needs. For `svc-core-banking-sync`, that destination is planned as a single **Azure Private Endpoint** in front of the core-banking sync service -- not a broad subnet CIDR range, not "anything in the core-banking resource group," one specific private IP behind one specific NSG rule. The same pattern applies to the other two exempted accounts, each mapped to its own single, named destination.

This is planned explicitly as a compensating control for the MFA exception, not a general-purpose segmentation rollout -- the pilot's entire scope, for now, is the three accounts already named in `CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt`. That scoping choice matters: a pilot that tried to segment the whole network at once would take months and delay the one piece of risk reduction the three riskiest identities in the tenant actually need first. The plan is honest about what this control does and doesn't do: it does not make a stolen `svc-core-banking-sync` credential harmless -- whoever holds it can still authenticate and reach the one core-banking endpoint it's allowed to reach, with whatever access that account legitimately has there. What it prevents is that credential being used as a foothold to reach anything *else* on Oakmere's network -- no lateral movement into branch systems, reporting infrastructure, or anywhere outside that one allowed path. The plan also fixes a rollout order: provision and validate the default-deny baseline and the three explicit allows in a non-production environment first, confirm the three accounts' real workloads still function end-to-end against the restricted path, and only then promote the same NSG rules to production -- a segmentation rule that silently breaks the account's own legitimate traffic is a worse outcome than not having the control at all.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Inventory exactly what each exempted account actually needs to reach

```text
ACCOUNT                      REQUIRED DESTINATION (and nothing else)
svc-core-banking-sync        Private Endpoint: pe-core-banking-sync (10.40.2.15/32)
svc-branch-reporting-sync    Private Endpoint: pe-branch-reporting-etl (10.40.3.22/32)
svc-atm-settlement-batch     Private Endpoint: pe-atm-settlement (10.40.4.9/32)
```

## Step 2 -- Plan the default-deny NSG baseline

```text
# planned NSG shape, not yet applied
subnet: snet-legacy-service-accounts
  default rule: DenyAllOutbound (priority 4096, deny, any -> any)
  default rule: DenyAllInbound  (priority 4096, deny, any -> any)
```

## Step 3 -- Plan the one explicit allow rule per account

```json
{
  "securityRules": [
    {
      "name": "Allow-svc-core-banking-sync-to-CoreBankingPE",
      "priority": 100,
      "direction": "Outbound",
      "access": "Allow",
      "protocol": "Tcp",
      "sourceAddressPrefix": "10.40.1.11/32",
      "destinationAddressPrefix": "10.40.2.15/32",
      "destinationPortRange": "443"
    }
  ]
}
```

Same pattern, repeated once per account, each with its own single source IP and single destination private endpoint -- no shared or broad rules.

## Step 4 -- Plan the Private Endpoint in front of the core-banking sync service

```text
# planned shape
resource: pe-core-banking-sync
  target service: core-banking-sync-svc (internal)
  approved connections: svc-core-banking-sync workload subnet only
  public network access: disabled
```

## Step 5 -- Plan the rollout order

```text
1. Apply default-deny baseline + the three explicit allows in a non-prod
   subnet mirroring production.
2. Run each legacy account's actual scheduled job against the restricted
   path; confirm it completes successfully end to end.
3. Confirm, by testing, that traffic to any destination other than the
   one named endpoint is actually blocked for each account.
4. Only after both checks pass, promote the identical NSG rules to the
   production subnet.
```

## Step 6 -- Name what this pilot does not claim to fix

```text
This pilot does NOT:
  - Remove the need for the MFA exception's own compensating review
    (quarterly access review from the last lesson still applies).
  - Protect data or access at the one endpoint each account is still
    allowed to reach -- a stolen credential still works there.
  - Segment the rest of Oakmere's network -- scope is the three
    CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt accounts only, for this pilot.
```

Renata brings this plan to the network engineering lead and the core banking engineering owner for `svc-core-banking-sync` specifically, to confirm the one allowed destination is actually complete -- missing a legitimate destination here means a real job breaks the moment this pilot goes live.

Planned rollout order (non-prod validation before prod promotion) and explicitly scoped this as lateral-movement containment, not a fix for credential theft at the one allowed destination.

lessons.title: Architecting the Python Automation and SOAR Ticketing Pipeline
lessons.summary: Planning ip-reputation-enrichment.py as a scheduled Azure Automation Runbook that independently cross-references sign-in logs against a threat-intel feed and opens a ticket -- a detection layer deliberately built separate from Sentinel's own analytics rules.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Sentinel's analytics rules -- including the detection architecture already planned for `law-oakmere-soc` -- are Oakmere's primary, near-real-time line of defense against bad sign-ins. This lesson plans a second, deliberately independent line: a Python script, **`ip-reputation-enrichment.py`**, running as a scheduled **Azure Automation Runbook**. Once a day, it's planned to pull recent sign-in activity, cross-reference every source IP against a threat-intelligence IP reputation feed, and -- on a match -- open a real ticket in the SOC's ticketing queue rather than just writing a log line nobody reads.

The design decision this lesson spends the most time on is *why this runs separately from Sentinel's own rule logic at all*, instead of just becoming another Sentinel analytics rule. The answer is architectural humility: any single detection method, including a well-built Sentinel rule, can have a scoping mistake or a blind spot nobody's found yet. Building a second method -- different data path, different logic, different cadence -- means a gap in one doesn't automatically become a gap in both. This lesson plans the runbook, its schedule, its data sources, and its ticketing handoff. It does not yet claim this script catches everything Sentinel's rules might miss, and it says so plainly: it's a daily batch job, not a real-time control, and that tradeoff is deliberate, not an oversight.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a store that already has an alarm system wired to every door and window -- that's the fast, automatic system. On top of that, imagine the night manager also walks through the visitor sign-in sheet every morning and compares every name against a list of known troublemakers from other stores in town, using nothing but her own eyes and that list -- a completely different method than the alarm system uses. If the alarm has a blind spot nobody noticed yet, her morning check is a second, independent chance to catch the same intruder a different way.

That's the automation Renata plans here. Once a day, a script checks every sign-in against a list of IP addresses already known to be bad, using a totally different approach than Sentinel's own rules. If it finds a match, it doesn't just make a note -- it opens a real ticket that lands in front of a person on the SOC team. It's planned honestly, too: once a day isn't instant, and this lesson says so, rather than pretending a daily check is the same thing as an alarm that goes off immediately.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The runbook is planned to run inside an **Azure Automation Account** already provisioned for Oakmere's security tooling, using a **system-assigned managed identity** scoped with Log Analytics Reader access against `law-oakmere-soc` -- no stored credentials inside the script itself. On a daily schedule, the script queries the prior 24 hours of sign-in activity (planned against the `SigninLogs` table once the workspace and connectors from the next lesson are live), extracts the distinct source IP addresses, and checks each one against a threat-intelligence IP reputation feed via a REST lookup. Any IP that comes back flagged gets written to a structured finding -- account, IP, timestamp, feed confidence score -- and that finding is POSTed to the SOC's ticketing system's REST API, creating a real, assigned ticket rather than a log entry.

The cadence is planned as daily, deliberately, not as a limitation nobody noticed. A near-real-time Sentinel rule and a daily batch reconciliation job answer different questions: the rule asks "does this sign-in look wrong right now," and the script asks "does yesterday's sign-in activity, in hindsight and against the freshest threat intelligence, look wrong." Building the second method with its own data path -- a direct KQL query against sign-in logs, rather than consuming Sentinel's own alert output -- means it doesn't inherit any scoping decision baked into a specific analytics rule. That independence is the entire point: if a rule's exclusion logic is ever too broad in some way nobody's caught yet, this script's cross-reference against sign-in logs runs on its own terms and isn't filtered by that rule at all. This lesson plans that architecture and states its honest limits -- daily, not real-time, and a reasonable but not exhaustive IP reputation feed -- rather than presenting it as a complete safety net.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Provision the Automation Account identity, in the plan

```bash
# planned shape, not yet applied
az automation account create \
  --name aa-oakmere-soc-automation \
  --resource-group rg-oakmere-soc \
  --location eastus

az automation account identity assign \
  --name aa-oakmere-soc-automation \
  --resource-group rg-oakmere-soc

# Grant the managed identity Log Analytics Reader on law-oakmere-soc
az role assignment create \
  --assignee <automation-account-principal-id> \
  --role "Log Analytics Reader" \
  --scope /subscriptions/<sub-id>/resourceGroups/rg-oakmere-soc/providers/Microsoft.OperationalInsights/workspaces/law-oakmere-soc
```

## Step 2 -- Plan the runbook's query and cross-reference logic

```python
# ip-reputation-enrichment.py -- planned structure, Azure Automation Runbook (Python)
import requests
from azure.identity import ManagedIdentityCredential
from azure.monitor.query import LogsQueryClient

WORKSPACE_ID = "<law-oakmere-soc-workspace-id>"
TI_FEED_API = "https://ti-feed.example.com/v1/ip-reputation"

SIGNIN_QUERY = """
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| distinct UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, Location
"""

def get_recent_signin_ips():
    credential = ManagedIdentityCredential()
    client = LogsQueryClient(credential)
    response = client.query_workspace(WORKSPACE_ID, SIGNIN_QUERY, timespan=None)
    return [
        {"user": row.UserPrincipalName, "ip": row.IPAddress, "location": row.Location}
        for table in response.tables for row in table.rows
    ]

def check_ip_reputation(ip_address):
    resp = requests.get(TI_FEED_API, params={"ip": ip_address}, timeout=10)
    resp.raise_for_status()
    return resp.json()  # { "malicious": bool, "confidence": int, "category": str }
```

## Step 3 -- Plan the finding and the ticket it creates

```python
def open_soc_ticket(finding):
    ticket_payload = {
        "title": f"IP reputation match: {finding['ip']} ({finding['category']})",
        "description": (
            f"Account {finding['user']} signed in from {finding['ip']} "
            f"({finding['location']}), flagged by threat-intel feed with "
            f"confidence {finding['confidence']}."
        ),
        "severity": "high" if finding["confidence"] >= 80 else "medium",
        "source": "ip-reputation-enrichment.py",
    }
    requests.post("https://soc-ticketing.oakmere.internal/api/tickets", json=ticket_payload, timeout=10)

def run():
    for signin in get_recent_signin_ips():
        rep = check_ip_reputation(signin["ip"])
        if rep["malicious"]:
            open_soc_ticket({**signin, **rep})

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()
```

## Step 4 -- Plan the daily schedule

```bash
# planned schedule, not yet created
az automation schedule create \
  --automation-account-name aa-oakmere-soc-automation \
  --resource-group rg-oakmere-soc \
  --name daily-ip-reputation-check \
  --frequency Day --interval 1 --start-time "2026-11-01T06:00:00Z"

az automation runbook create \
  --automation-account-name aa-oakmere-soc-automation \
  --resource-group rg-oakmere-soc \
  --name ip-reputation-enrichment \
  --type Python3
```

## Step 5 -- Write down why this is independent, and what it isn't

```text
DESIGN RATIONALE:
  - Queries SigninLogs directly -- does not consume Sentinel's own alert
    output, so a scoping gap in any one Sentinel rule does not filter
    what this script sees.
  - Runs daily, in batch -- NOT a real-time control. This is a stated
    tradeoff, not an unnoticed limitation.
  - Opens a real, assigned ticket on a match -- a finding nobody reads
    is the same as no finding at all.
  - Does not claim to catch every failure mode Sentinel's rules might
    miss -- it is one additional, independent layer, reviewed and
    improved over time, not a finished safety net.
```

Renata brings this architecture to the SOC lead and the identity team before building it: does the daily cadence fit how quickly the team can act on a ticket, and does Log Analytics Reader give the managed identity everything it needs without granting anything broader than that single query requires.

Deliberately architected independent of Sentinel's own rule logic and alert output, with the daily batch cadence and its limits stated explicitly rather than presented as real-time coverage.

lessons.title: Deploying the Sentinel Workspace and Data Connectors
lessons.summary: The first real implementation step -- standing up the law-oakmere-soc Log Analytics workspace, enabling Microsoft Sentinel on it, and connecting Entra ID, Defender XDR, Azure Activity, and AWS CloudTrail so real signal finally starts flowing in.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Every lesson so far has been a plan -- the MFA policy, the segmentation pilot, the Python automation's architecture. This lesson is where Renata Ibarra actually builds something: the real **Log Analytics workspace, `law-oakmere-soc`**, with **Microsoft Sentinel** enabled directly on top of it, and four data connectors wired in so real security signal starts landing in one place for the first time. The four connectors are **Entra ID** (sign-in and audit logs), **Microsoft Defender XDR**, **Azure Activity** logs, and **AWS CloudTrail** (via Sentinel's AWS S3 connector, reading CloudTrail logs delivered to an S3 bucket through a cross-account IAM role).

This lesson is scoped to infrastructure and ingestion only. No analytics rule gets written here -- not the Impossible Travel rule, not anything else. Building a detection rule against a workspace that isn't confirmed to actually be receiving data would be building on a guess; this lesson's job is to stand up the workspace, wire in the connectors, and prove -- with a real query, against real rows -- that data is actually arriving before any detection logic gets built on top of it in the lesson ahead.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine building a brand-new security control room for a bank: wiring up the room so it can record, turning on the recording system itself, and plugging in the cameras from the lobby, the vault, the parking lot, and a partner building across town -- all before anyone writes a single rule like "ring the alarm if a camera sees this." You wouldn't write that alarm rule until you'd confirmed every camera is actually sending a picture to the room; a rule pointed at a camera that isn't even plugged in would never catch anything, and nobody would know why.

That's this lesson. Renata builds the actual control room -- the workspace -- turns on Sentinel, and plugs in four real sources of signal: sign-ins and account activity from Entra ID, alerts from Defender, Azure's own activity logs, and AWS's activity logs. Then she checks, carefully, that real information is actually showing up from each one. Writing the actual alarm rules comes next, once the cameras are confirmed to be on.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The workspace is provisioned first, since Sentinel is a solution layered onto an existing Log Analytics workspace rather than a standalone resource -- `law-oakmere-soc` is created with a retention period matching Oakmere's regulatory requirements, and the Microsoft Sentinel solution is then enabled against that same workspace ID. Connector wiring follows a consistent pattern across sources, but the mechanics differ meaningfully by source.

The **Entra ID connector** is enabled by configuring diagnostic settings on the tenant to stream `SignInLogs` and `AuditLogs` categories directly to `law-oakmere-soc` -- this is the exact table the Impossible Travel rule and the Python automation's daily query both depend on, so its correct configuration here is load-bearing for everything downstream. The **Defender XDR connector** is a native, built-in Sentinel integration -- enabling it streams Defender's own incidents and alerts into the workspace without a separate diagnostic-settings step. The **Azure Activity connector** is wired through a diagnostic setting at the subscription level, exporting management-plane activity (resource changes, role assignments, and so on) into the same workspace. The **AWS CloudTrail connector** is the most involved: it depends on a cross-account IAM role in the AWS account that trusts Sentinel's AWS connector principal, an SQS queue that gets notified when new CloudTrail log files land in the S3 bucket, and Sentinel's AWS S3 connector configured with that role ARN and queue URL -- CloudTrail logs land in `AWSCloudTrail` once this is correctly wired.

The lesson's actual deliverable, beyond the resources themselves, is verified ingestion: a KQL query against each of the four relevant tables, confirming real rows with a recent `TimeGenerated` timestamp, run and checked before this lesson is considered done. A connector that shows "connected" in the Sentinel UI but isn't actually producing queryable rows is a false confirmation, and this lesson treats the query result, not the UI status indicator, as the real source of truth.
