lessons.title: Building the Impossible Travel Analytics Rule in Microsoft Sentinel
lessons.summary: Renata Ibarra and Senior SOC Analyst Priya Desai build the real KQL for "Impossible Travel - Interactive Sign-ins" in law-oakmere-soc, then scope it to exclude any account tagged ServiceAccount in a watchlist, so Oakmere's routine automation traffic stops flooding the SOC queue with false positives.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With the Sentinel workspace `law-oakmere-soc` connected to Oakmere Credit Union's Entra sign-in and audit logs in the last lesson, this lesson writes the first real detection on top of that data: a Microsoft Sentinel analytics rule named **"Impossible Travel - Interactive Sign-ins."** The rule's job is straightforward and genuinely useful -- it looks at every successful, interactive sign-in for a user, compares it against that same user's other recent sign-ins, and does the geometry: if two sign-ins happened far enough apart, in too short a window, for a real human to have physically traveled between them, it flags the pair.

The rule Renata and Priya Desai, a Senior SOC Analyst, build here is real, working KQL against the `SigninLogs` table in `law-oakmere-soc` -- distance calculated with `geo_distance_2points`, speed derived from distance over elapsed time, thresholded above what a commercial flight could realistically cover. But the moment they run it against real tenant traffic, it's immediately clear the rule as written is far too noisy to be usable: Oakmere's own scheduled service accounts -- backup jobs, kiosk-management sync tools, and others -- authenticate from multiple Azure regions and on-prem sites within minutes of each other as a completely normal part of how they're built, and every one of those legitimate automation patterns trips the rule. The fix they land on is a tag-based exclusion: a Sentinel watchlist, `ServiceAccountTags`, listing every account across the tenant tagged `ServiceAccount`, filtered out of the rule entirely before the travel-distance logic ever runs. It is, at this point in the project, a reasonable and common way to cut that specific kind of noise -- and it is also the exact decision this series will need to revisit much later, once a compromise shows exactly what a tag that broad lets through unnoticed.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a hallway monitor whose only job is to notice if the same kid shows up at two doors on opposite ends of the school in under a minute -- that's clearly impossible, so it's worth a closer look. That's the rule Renata and Priya build: it watches for one person logging in from two places too far apart, too fast, to really be the same person doing it normally.

But when they turn the monitor on, it starts going off constantly -- because some of the "kids" aren't kids at all, they're robots doing scheduled chores, and the robots really do move between far-apart doors in seconds because that's just how they're built to run. So Renata and Priya give the monitor a list of which badges belong to robots, and tell it to ignore anyone wearing one of those badges completely. That solves the noise problem today. Whether a sneaky person could ever borrow a robot's badge and walk right past the monitor unnoticed isn't a question this lesson is asking yet.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The detection logic itself is solid, standard impossible-travel construction: a self-join of `SigninLogs` against itself on `UserPrincipalName`, restricted to successful (`ResultType == "0"`), interactive (`IsInteractive == true`) sign-ins, with `geo_distance_2points` computing the great-circle distance between each pair's latitude/longitude and a derived `ImpliedSpeedKmh` thresholded above what a commercial flight could cover. That part of the rule is not the issue, and it won't need revisiting later in this series.

The exclusion is where the real engineering tradeoff lives. Oakmere's scheduled automation -- a Veeam backup job, a branch-kiosk management sync, a handful of other service accounts -- genuinely does authenticate from multiple Azure regions and on-prem sites within minutes, as an intended property of how those jobs are architected, not a bug. Run unfiltered, the rule fires on that pattern dozens of times a day, and a SOC that triages dozens of false positives daily stops trusting -- and eventually stops looking at -- the rule at all. Renata and Priya's fix is to maintain a Sentinel watchlist, `ServiceAccountTags`, tagging every account across the tenant that's a known piece of automation, and excluding any `UserPrincipalName` that appears in it before the travel-distance logic ever evaluates. This is a completely defensible, widely used pattern for this exact noise problem, and it is scoped at the account level rather than at the level of *which specific sign-ins from that account are actually non-interactive* -- a simpler, more maintainable rule to write and operate today, at the cost of a broader exclusion than the narrowest version of the fix would require. That gap between "excludes the account" and "excludes only the automated, non-interactive traffic from the account" is not evaluated or stress-tested in this lesson. It is simply the shape of the decision as it's made here, with the information Renata and Priya have at this point in the build.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Confirm the data the rule needs is already flowing

Before writing the rule, Renata confirms `SigninLogs` is populating in `law-oakmere-soc` from the Entra ID connector set up in the previous lesson:

```kql
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where IsInteractive == true
| count
```

## Step 2 -- Write the first version of the rule, with no exclusion

```kql
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "0" and IsInteractive == true
| extend Lat = toreal(LocationDetails.geoCoordinates.latitude),
         Lon = toreal(LocationDetails.geoCoordinates.longitude)
| where isnotempty(Lat) and isnotempty(Lon)
| join kind=inner (
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType == "0" and IsInteractive == true
    | extend Lat = toreal(LocationDetails.geoCoordinates.latitude),
             Lon = toreal(LocationDetails.geoCoordinates.longitude)
) on UserPrincipalName
| where TimeGenerated1 > TimeGenerated
| extend DistanceKm = geo_distance_2points(Lon, Lat, Lon1, Lat1) / 1000
| where DistanceKm > 500
```

Running this against real tenant data immediately returns dozens of hits a day, almost all from automation accounts, not people.

```
PRIYA:    Look at this -- svc-backup-veeam shows up eleven times
          overnight. It's not impossible travel, it's a backup job
          replicating out of three regions on a schedule. Same story
          with the kiosk-management sync account.

RENATA:   So the rule logic is right, we just need it to leave
          automation alone. How do we tell the rule which accounts
          are actually people versus scripts?

PRIYA:    Easiest maintainable way is a watchlist. We already tag
          every service account as "ServiceAccount" in our asset
          inventory -- let's mirror that tag into Sentinel and
          exclude on it.
```

## Step 3 -- Build the ServiceAccountTags watchlist

In Sentinel, under **Watchlists -> Add new**, Renata creates `ServiceAccountTags` from a CSV covering every account across the Oakmere tenant already tagged as automation in the asset inventory:

```csv
UserPrincipalName,Tag,Owner
svc-backup-veeam@oakmere-cu.onmicrosoft.com,ServiceAccount,Infrastructure
svc-core-banking-sync@oakmere-cu.onmicrosoft.com,ServiceAccount,Core Banking
svc-branch-kiosk-mgmt@oakmere-cu.onmicrosoft.com,ServiceAccount,Branch Ops
svc-print-services@oakmere-cu.onmicrosoft.com,ServiceAccount,IT Operations
svc-ad-sync-connector@oakmere-cu.onmicrosoft.com,ServiceAccount,Identity
... (42 more rows -- every account the tenant's asset inventory tags
    as a scheduled job, sync connector, or automation identity)
```

```
RENATA:   That's 47 accounts total once I pull the full export. The
          core banking sync job is in here too, obviously -- it runs
          on a schedule same as the rest.

PRIYA:    Makes sense, it's tagged ServiceAccount in the inventory
          just like the others. Exclude the whole watchlist and this
          rule should go quiet on the automation noise.
```

## Step 4 -- Finalize the rule with the exclusion

```kql
// =====================================================================
// Analytics Rule: Impossible Travel - Interactive Sign-ins
// Workspace: law-oakmere-soc   |   Tenant: oakmere-cu
// Purpose:   Flag a user account with two successful INTERACTIVE
//            sign-ins from locations far enough apart that the time
//            between them makes real physical travel impossible.
// Exclusion: Any UserPrincipalName tagged "ServiceAccount" in the
//            ServiceAccountTags watchlist is excluded from this rule
//            entirely. Rationale: Oakmere's scheduled/automated
//            service accounts routinely authenticate from multiple
//            Azure regions and on-prem data centers within minutes of
//            each other as part of normal, expected automation -- left
//            unfiltered, this rule fires on that pattern constantly and
//            drowns the SOC queue in noise that isn't a real threat.
// =====================================================================
let lookback = 1d;
let speedThresholdKmh = 1000;      // faster than a commercial jet
let minDistanceKm = 500;           // ignore noise between nearby cities
let ServiceAccountUPNs =
    (_GetWatchlist('ServiceAccountTags')
     | where Tag == "ServiceAccount"
     | project UserPrincipalName);
let Signins =
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
    | where ResultType == "0"                          // successful only
    | where IsInteractive == true                       // interactive only
    | where UserPrincipalName !in (ServiceAccountUPNs)   // <-- the exclusion
    | extend Lat = toreal(LocationDetails.geoCoordinates.latitude),
             Lon = toreal(LocationDetails.geoCoordinates.longitude),
             City = tostring(LocationDetails.city),
             Country = tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion)
    | where isnotempty(Lat) and isnotempty(Lon)
    | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, City, Country, Lat, Lon;
Signins
| join kind=inner (Signins) on UserPrincipalName
| where TimeGenerated1 > TimeGenerated
| extend DistanceKm = geo_distance_2points(Lon, Lat, Lon1, Lat1) / 1000
| where DistanceKm > minDistanceKm
| extend HoursBetween = datetime_diff('minute', TimeGenerated1, TimeGenerated) / 60.0
| extend ImpliedSpeedKmh = DistanceKm / HoursBetween
| where ImpliedSpeedKmh > speedThresholdKmh
| project UserPrincipalName,
          FirstSeenTime = TimeGenerated, FirstCity = City, FirstIP = IPAddress,
          SecondSeenTime = TimeGenerated1, SecondCity = City1, SecondIP = IPAddress1,
          DistanceKm, HoursBetween, ImpliedSpeedKmh
| sort by ImpliedSpeedKmh desc
```

## Step 5 -- Configure the analytics rule in Sentinel

```
Rule name:            Impossible Travel - Interactive Sign-ins
Rule frequency:       Run every 1 hour
Lookup data from:     Last 24 hours
Alert threshold:      Trigger when results > 0
Severity:             High
MITRE ATT&CK tactics: Initial Access, Credential Access
Entity mapping:       Account -> UserPrincipalName, IP -> SecondIP
```

## Step 6 -- Validate against real traffic and sign off

```
PRIYA:    Ran it for the last 24 hours with the exclusion in place --
          zero false positives from automation, and it still catches
          the test case we staged with two different VPN exit
          countries on the same test account.

RENATA:   Good, that's a clean signal-to-noise tradeoff for now. I'll
          document the watchlist as the thing to keep current --
          if a new service account goes live and nobody tags it,
          we're back to noise; if an existing one somehow shouldn't
          be trusted blindly, that's a conversation for another day.
```

Renata documents the rule, the watchlist, and the exclusion rationale in the SOC runbook, and the rule goes live in `law-oakmere-soc` ahead of the Conditional Access work in the next lesson.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Built and deployed the "Impossible Travel - Interactive Sign-ins" analytics rule in law-oakmere-soc: a self-join on SigninLogs using geo_distance_2points and a 1000 km/h implied-speed threshold, restricted to successful interactive sign-ins, running hourly over a 24-hour lookback. Added a ServiceAccountTags watchlist (47 accounts, including svc-core-banking-sync) and excluded the whole watchlist from the rule to eliminate false positives from scheduled automation.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Renata and Priya built our first real detection rule for suspicious sign-in locations and tuned it against real traffic until it stopped falsely flagging our own backup and sync jobs. It's live and validated against a test case.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We now have an automated system watching for logins that couldn't physically be the real employee -- for example, a login from two countries within minutes of each other. We tuned it so it doesn't cry wolf over our own routine automated processes.

lessons.title: Configuring Conditional Access: Tenant-Wide MFA and the Legacy Service Account Exemption
lessons.summary: Renata and Identity & Access Engineer Grace Liu roll out CA-RequireMFA-AllUsers across the oakmere-cu tenant, then carve out one temporary, scoped exclusion -- CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt -- for three service accounts still migrating off legacy auth, including svc-core-banking-sync.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With a real detection rule now watching for impossible sign-in travel, this lesson closes the other half of the identity story: making sure the vast majority of sign-ins actually require multi-factor authentication in the first place. Renata works with Grace Liu, Oakmere's Identity & Access Engineer, to roll out a single, tenant-wide Conditional Access policy, **`CA-RequireMFA-AllUsers`**, in the `oakmere-cu` Entra tenant: all users, all cloud apps, grant control set to require MFA.

A blanket policy like that, applied with zero exceptions, breaks things on day one -- and it does here too. Three legacy service accounts, still mid-migration onto modern authentication, fail immediately: they authenticate through older connectors and scheduled jobs that have no way to complete an MFA challenge at all, because nothing is sitting at a keyboard to approve one. Rather than quietly disabling MFA tenant-wide or hand-exempting accounts ad hoc, Grace and Renata build one scoped, named exclusion group, **`CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt`**, add exactly the three accounts that need it -- including `svc-core-banking-sync` -- and attach that group as the policy's only exclusion. It is a standard, temporary migration pattern used constantly during real MFA rollouts, done here with a plan to retire it once those three accounts move to certificate-based or managed-identity auth -- not a permanent hole left open by accident.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a school decides every single person who walks in the front door, no exceptions, has to show a hall pass. Great rule -- except there are three delivery robots that restock the vending machines every morning before anyone else arrives, and robots can't hold a hall pass. So instead of turning off the hall-pass rule for everyone, or just quietly waving the robots through one at a time, the school makes one official list -- "the three delivery robots" -- and tells the front door to let only those three through without a pass, while everyone and everything else still needs one.

That's exactly what Renata and Grace do. Almost everyone at Oakmere now needs a second proof of identity to log in. Three specific automated accounts, including the one that keeps the core banking system in sync, are on one named, written-down list that's excused from that rule for now, because they genuinely can't complete that extra step yet -- with a plan to fix that properly later.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Conditional Access is configured the standard way: `CA-RequireMFA-AllUsers` targets `includeUsers: All`, `includeApplications: All`, with a grant control of `builtInControls: ["mfa"]` -- the broadest, simplest MFA baseline Entra supports, and the right starting point for a tenant that previously had no consistent MFA enforcement at all.

The exclusion decision is where the real judgment call sits. Three accounts -- `svc-core-banking-sync`, `svc-backup-veeam`, and `svc-branch-kiosk-mgmt` -- are mid-migration onto certificate-based or managed-identity authentication but still, today, authenticate through connectors that have no mechanism to satisfy an MFA challenge: there is no interactive session to push an approval to. Grace and Renata's response is deliberately not to carve individual per-account policy exceptions, and not to quietly turn off enforcement tenant-wide -- both would be worse. Instead they create one named, auditable group, `CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt`, add exactly those three accounts, and scope the exclusion to that group alone in the policy's `excludeGroups` condition. That gives the SOC one place to look to answer "who is exempt from MFA and why" instead of scattered, undocumented exceptions -- and it's a textbook, widely-used way to stage an MFA rollout around legacy systems that genuinely can't support it yet, with a tracked remediation plan rather than an open-ended exception. What this lesson does not do is evaluate what *else* depends on, or interacts with, membership in that group -- including whether anything else in the environment also keys off these same three accounts' exempt status for a different kind of decision. That's outside this lesson's scope.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Attempt the blanket policy and watch it break something real

In the Entra admin center, under **Protection -> Conditional Access**, Grace creates the baseline policy first, with no exclusions:

```
Policy name:        CA-RequireMFA-AllUsers
Users:              Include: All users
Cloud apps:         Include: All cloud apps
Conditions:         (none additional for V1)
Grant:              Require multi-factor authentication
Enable policy:      On
```

Within minutes of enabling it in report-only mode and then live, three accounts start failing sign-in:

```
GRACE:    svc-core-banking-sync just failed its scheduled 2 a.m. sync
          -- MFA challenge, no one there to approve it. Same with the
          Veeam backup job and the kiosk-management sync overnight.

RENATA:   That tracks -- none of those are interactive sessions, so
          there's no device to push an MFA prompt to in the first
          place. We can't leave the whole tenant without MFA over
          three accounts, but we also can't just leave their jobs
          broken.
```

## Step 2 -- Confirm which accounts actually need the exception, and why

```
GRACE:   Pulling the migration tracker -- these three are specifically
         flagged as "legacy auth, migration in progress": core-banking-
         sync, the Veeam backup account, and branch-kiosk-mgmt. All
         three are scheduled to move to cert-based or managed-identity
         auth, just not yet. Everything else tagged ServiceAccount in
         our inventory already supports modern auth and doesn't need
         an exception at all.

RENATA:  So this is three accounts, not the whole ServiceAccount tag
         list -- good, let's keep the exclusion as narrow as the real
         need.
```

## Step 3 -- Create the exclusion group

```powershell
# Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "Group.ReadWrite.All","Directory.ReadWrite.All"

New-MgGroup -DisplayName "CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt" `
  -MailEnabled:$false `
  -MailNickname "ca-legacy-svc-exempt" `
  -SecurityEnabled:$true `
  -Description "Temporary CA-RequireMFA-AllUsers exclusion for legacy service accounts still migrating off legacy auth. Owner: Grace Liu. Review before Q1 close."

$groupId = (Get-MgGroup -Filter "displayName eq 'CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt'").Id

$legacyAccounts = @(
  "svc-core-banking-sync@oakmere-cu.onmicrosoft.com",
  "svc-backup-veeam@oakmere-cu.onmicrosoft.com",
  "svc-branch-kiosk-mgmt@oakmere-cu.onmicrosoft.com"
)

foreach ($upn in $legacyAccounts) {
  $user = Get-MgUser -Filter "userPrincipalName eq '$upn'"
  New-MgGroupMember -GroupId $groupId -DirectoryObjectId $user.Id
}
```

## Step 4 -- Attach the exclusion to the policy

```json
{
  "displayName": "CA-RequireMFA-AllUsers",
  "state": "enabled",
  "conditions": {
    "users": {
      "includeUsers": ["All"],
      "excludeGroups": ["<CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt group object ID>"]
    },
    "applications": {
      "includeApplications": ["All"]
    }
  },
  "grantControls": {
    "operator": "OR",
    "builtInControls": ["mfa"]
  }
}
```

## Step 5 -- Re-validate and schedule the remediation

```
GRACE:    All three accounts are back to running cleanly overnight,
          and the policy's report-only logs show everyone else is
          still being challenged for MFA exactly as expected.

RENATA:   I'll open a tracked backlog item to move all three onto
          certificate-based or managed-identity auth so this
          exclusion group can go away entirely -- it should be a
          migration step, not a permanent exception.
```

## Step 6 -- Document and sign off

Grace documents `CA-RequireMFA-AllUsers` and the `CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt` group -- membership, owner, and the planned remediation -- in the identity runbook, and both are live in the `oakmere-cu` tenant ahead of the cross-cloud IAM hardening work in the next lesson.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Deployed CA-RequireMFA-AllUsers (all users, all cloud apps, require MFA) tenant-wide in oakmere-cu. Created CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt as the policy's sole excludeGroups target, containing exactly three accounts mid-migration off legacy auth -- svc-core-banking-sync, svc-backup-veeam, svc-branch-kiosk-mgmt -- with a tracked backlog item to retire the exclusion once they move to certificate-based/managed-identity auth.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: MFA is now required tenant-wide for everyone, with one narrow, documented, temporary exception for three legacy automation accounts that can't yet complete an MFA challenge. We've logged a follow-up to close that exception once those accounts finish migrating.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Every person signing into Oakmere's systems now has to prove their identity a second way, closing a major door attackers use to get in with just a stolen password. Three old automated accounts still mid-upgrade are temporarily excused, with a plan already in place to bring them up to the same standard.

lessons.title: Hardening Identity Side by Side: Azure AD Least Privilege and AWS IAM
lessons.summary: Grace Liu and Renata apply least-privilege roles and periodic access reviews in Entra, build matching least-privilege IAM roles for Oakmere's AWS footprint, and federate AWS IAM Identity Center to the oakmere-cu tenant so both clouds answer to one identity source instead of two separate sets of standing credentials.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Oakmere Credit Union doesn't run on Azure alone -- a handful of workloads, including backup archival storage and a reporting data lake, live in AWS. This lesson takes the identity hardening started with Conditional Access and extends it across both clouds at once. On the Entra side, Grace Liu replaces several standing broad role assignments -- SOC and infrastructure staff who'd been handed `Global Administrator` or `Security Administrator` outright -- with narrower built-in and custom roles scoped to what each role actually needs day to day, made eligible rather than always-on through Privileged Identity Management (PIM), and reviewed on a recurring cadence through Entra Access Reviews.

On the AWS side, Renata and Grace apply the same least-privilege discipline to the IAM roles backing Oakmere's AWS workloads, replacing a handful of overly broad policies with tightly scoped ones built around what each workload actually calls. Then, rather than leaving AWS as a second, separately managed set of human credentials, they federate **AWS IAM Identity Center** to the `oakmere-cu` Entra tenant, so Oakmere's staff sign into AWS with the same Entra identity, the same MFA policy, and the same audit trail as everything else -- one identity source consolidating both clouds, instead of two.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a credit union where some employees were handed a master key that opens every door in the building, every vault, every filing cabinet, just because it was easier than cutting separate keys for each room they actually needed. That's risky -- if that one master key is ever copied or stolen, the thief gets everything, instantly. So the credit union does two things: first, it cuts proper, narrow keys that only open the rooms each person actually works in, and it makes someone officially check out even those keys for a shift rather than carrying them around all day forever. Second, it notices the credit union also has a second building across town (that's AWS) with its own separate set of keys and locks -- and instead of managing two completely different key systems forever, it links the two buildings' security desks together, so one ID badge works at both front doors, under the same rules.

That's what Grace and Renata build here: narrower, checked-out-only access instead of permanent master keys inside Entra, matching narrow access rules inside AWS, and one shared identity system linking both.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The Entra work follows the standard least-privilege remediation pattern once over-broad role assignments are found: Grace inventories every standing `Global Administrator` and `Security Administrator` assignment, re-maps each person's actual day-to-day tasks to the narrowest built-in role that covers them -- `Security Operator` for SOC analysts running and tuning Sentinel rules, a custom role scoped to exactly the identity-management permissions Grace's own work needs -- and converts those assignments from permanent to **PIM-eligible**, requiring a time-bound activation with justification rather than sitting active around the clock. A recurring Entra **Access Review**, run quarterly and owned by Grace, forces every privileged assignment to be re-justified or removed rather than silently accumulating as people change roles over time, which is the realistic failure mode standing privilege almost always degrades into if nothing forces a periodic re-check.

The AWS side gets the equivalent treatment at the IAM layer: Renata and Grace audit the policies attached to the roles backing Oakmere's backup-archival and reporting workloads, find several using AWS managed policies far broader than the workload's actual API surface (`AmazonS3FullAccess` where the workload only ever calls `s3:GetObject` and `s3:PutObject` against one specific bucket prefix), and replace them with customer-managed policies scoped to exactly those actions and resources. The more structurally important move is federating **AWS IAM Identity Center** to `oakmere-cu` as the identity source, so AWS console and CLI access for human staff flows through the same Entra identity, the same Conditional Access and MFA policy built in the previous lesson, and the same audit trail -- rather than AWS carrying its own, separately managed set of IAM users with their own passwords and their own MFA enrollment to track and eventually forget about. Consolidating identity this way doesn't change anything about how the Sentinel rule or the Conditional Access policy from the previous two lessons actually behave -- it's a separate, parallel hardening effort, not a fix to either of them.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Audit standing privileged role assignments in Entra

```powershell
# Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "RoleManagement.Read.Directory"
Get-MgRoleManagementDirectoryRoleAssignment -ExpandProperty "roleDefinition" |
  Where-Object { $_.RoleDefinition.DisplayName -in @("Global Administrator","Security Administrator") } |
  Select-Object PrincipalId, @{N="Role";E={$_.RoleDefinition.DisplayName}}
```

```
GRACE:    Eight people are sitting on permanent Global Administrator
          or Security Administrator today. Most of them only ever
          touch Sentinel rules, Conditional Access policies, or user
          lifecycle -- none of that needs the keys to the whole
          tenant, permanently, every hour of every day.
```

## Step 2 -- Re-map assignments to least-privilege, PIM-eligible roles

```powershell
# Example: move a SOC analyst from standing Security Administrator
# to PIM-eligible Security Operator (sufficient for running and
# tuning Sentinel analytics rules, incidents, and hunting queries).
New-MgRoleManagementDirectoryRoleEligibilityScheduleRequest -BodyParameter @{
  Action            = "adminAssign"
  Justification     = "Least-privilege remediation: SOC analyst role scoped to Security Operator, PIM-eligible, from standing Security Administrator."
  RoleDefinitionId  = "<Security Operator role definition ID>"
  PrincipalId       = "<Renata's object ID>"
  DirectoryScopeId  = "/"
  ScheduleInfo      = @{
    StartDateTime = (Get-Date)
    Expiration    = @{ Type = "noExpiration" }
  }
}
```

## Step 3 -- Build a quarterly Entra Access Review on every privileged role

```
Access review name:    Quarterly Privileged Role Review - oakmere-cu
Scope:                 Security Operator, Security Administrator,
                       Global Administrator, Conditional Access
                       Administrator
Reviewers:             Grace Liu (role owner) + each assignee self-
                       review
Recurrence:            Every 90 days
Auto-apply decisions:  On -- an unreviewed or denied assignment is
                       automatically removed at the end of the review
                       period
```

## Step 4 -- Audit the AWS side for the same over-broad pattern

```
RENATA:  Pulled the IAM policies attached to the backup-archival and
         reporting-datalake roles. Both are using AmazonS3FullAccess
         -- full access to every bucket in the account -- when the
         backup job only ever reads and writes to one bucket prefix,
         and the reporting job only ever reads from a different one.

GRACE:   Same pattern as Entra, just a different cloud. Let's scope
         both down to exactly what they call.
```

## Step 5 -- Replace the broad AWS managed policy with a scoped customer-managed policy

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "BackupArchivalLeastPrivilege",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "s3:GetObject",
        "s3:PutObject",
        "s3:ListBucket"
      ],
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:s3:::oakmere-backup-archive",
        "arn:aws:s3:::oakmere-backup-archive/nightly/*"
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

```bash
aws iam create-policy \
  --policy-name oakmere-backup-archival-least-privilege \
  --policy-document file://backup-archival-policy.json

aws iam detach-role-policy \
  --role-name oakmere-backup-archival-role \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonS3FullAccess

aws iam attach-role-policy \
  --role-name oakmere-backup-archival-role \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:policy/oakmere-backup-archival-least-privilege
```

## Step 6 -- Federate AWS IAM Identity Center to oakmere-cu

```
In AWS IAM Identity Center:
  Identity source:        External identity provider (SAML 2.0)
  IdP metadata:            Imported from Entra enterprise application
                           "AWS IAM Identity Center"
  Attribute mapping:       ${user.userprincipalname} -> Subject
In Entra (oakmere-cu):
  Enterprise application: AWS IAM Identity Center
  Assigned users/groups:  All staff with an existing AWS permission set
  Conditional Access:     CA-RequireMFA-AllUsers already applies --
                          no separate AWS-specific MFA policy needed
```

```
GRACE:    Now when anyone signs into the AWS console, they're
          authenticating against oakmere-cu, under the same MFA
          policy and the same sign-in logs we're already watching in
          law-oakmere-soc -- not a separate AWS password nobody's
          tracking.

RENATA:   That also means if that impossible-travel rule or any
          future Sentinel rule ever needs to reason about an AWS
          console sign-in, it's the same UserPrincipalName we're
          already working with, not a second identity to cross-
          reference.
```

## Step 7 -- Document and sign off

Grace documents the role re-mapping, the Access Review cadence, the AWS least-privilege policies, and the IAM Identity Center federation in the identity runbook, alongside `CA-RequireMFA-AllUsers` and `CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt` from the previous lesson, as the current state of identity hardening across both clouds.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Converted eight standing Global Administrator/Security Administrator assignments in oakmere-cu to least-privilege, PIM-eligible roles, backed by a quarterly Entra Access Review with auto-remove on unreviewed assignments. Replaced AmazonS3FullAccess on the backup-archival and reporting-datalake IAM roles with scoped customer-managed policies, and federated AWS IAM Identity Center to oakmere-cu via SAML so AWS console access runs through the same Entra identity and CA-RequireMFA-AllUsers policy.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We removed standing full-admin access for eight people and replaced it with narrower, time-limited access that's reviewed every quarter. We did the same cleanup on the AWS side and linked AWS sign-in to the same identity system we already use everywhere else, so there's one place to manage access instead of two.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Fewer people now carry permanent, all-access keys to our systems -- access is granted only for what each role actually needs, checked out rather than left on indefinitely, and reviewed every quarter. We also connected our AWS cloud environment to the same sign-in system as everything else, closing a gap where a second set of credentials could otherwise go unmonitored.

lessons.title: Building and Scheduling the ip-reputation-enrichment.py Automation
lessons.summary: Renata and Priya write ip-reputation-enrichment.py, a Python script that pulls every distinct sign-in IP from law-oakmere-soc, checks each against AbuseIPDB, writes malicious hits to a custom Sentinel log table, and runs it daily as an Azure Automation Runbook under a managed identity.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Not every useful security signal fits neatly into a real-time Sentinel analytics rule. Some enrichment is cheaper and more reliable to run as a scheduled batch job against an external data source -- which is exactly what this lesson builds. Renata and Priya Desai write **`ip-reputation-enrichment.py`**: a Python script that queries `law-oakmere-soc` for every distinct source IP address that authenticated against Oakmere's tenant in the last 24 hours, checks each one against a third-party threat-intelligence feed, **AbuseIPDB**, and writes any IP that crosses a malicious-confidence threshold into a dedicated custom log table in Sentinel, `IPReputationEnrichment_CL`, for the SOC to triage.

The script itself is real, working Python -- using the `azure-monitor-query` SDK to pull sign-in IPs, `requests` to call AbuseIPDB's reputation API, and the `azure-monitor-ingestion` SDK to write flagged results back into Sentinel through a Data Collection Rule. It authenticates to Azure using a managed identity rather than a stored secret, and it's deployed and scheduled to run automatically, once a day, as an **Azure Automation Runbook** -- no one has to remember to run it by hand. This gives the SOC a daily, independent check against outside threat intelligence, layered on top of the real-time Sentinel rule and the Conditional Access policy already built -- a different kind of coverage than either of those, running on its own schedule, against its own data source.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a credit union keeps a daily logbook of every visitor's car license plate that pulled into the parking lot. Every night, a clerk takes that whole list and calls a national hotline that keeps track of license plates reported as stolen or suspicious, checking each one. If the hotline says a plate is bad news, the clerk writes it down in a special "watch this one" book for the morning security team to look at first thing.

That's the robot Renata and Priya build. Every night, it quietly collects every IP address that logged into Oakmere's systems that day, asks a trusted outside service whether any of them are known to be bad, and writes down the ones that are, so the security team sees that list waiting for them the next morning -- without anyone having to remember to go check by hand.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The script is built around three real Azure SDKs rather than hand-rolled REST calls: `azure.monitor.query.LogsQueryClient` runs the KQL pull of distinct sign-in IPs from `law-oakmere-soc` (grouped by `IPAddress`, carrying a sample of affected `UserPrincipalName`s via `make_set`); `requests` calls AbuseIPDB's `/api/v2/check` endpoint per IP, reading back `abuseConfidenceScore` as the core signal; and `azure.monitor.ingestion.LogsIngestionClient` writes any IP scoring at or above the chosen threshold (75, a conservative bar above AbuseIPDB's noisier low-confidence reports) into `IPReputationEnrichment_CL` through a Data Collection Rule and Data Collection Endpoint, the modern, supported ingestion path for custom Sentinel tables.

Authentication is deliberately `ManagedIdentityCredential`, not a stored API key or client secret for Azure itself -- the Automation Account's system-assigned managed identity is granted `Log Analytics Reader` on `law-oakmere-soc` and a data-upload role scoped to the specific Data Collection Rule, and nothing Azure-side needs a secret sitting in a variable or a script. The one external credential that is unavoidable, the AbuseIPDB API key, lives in an Automation Account encrypted variable rather than inline in the script. Scheduling is handled the ordinary way for a Python 3 runbook in Azure Automation: published to the Automation Account, attached to a daily schedule at 02:00 UTC, run once against the previous 24 hours of sign-in activity every single day without any human in the loop. This is a general-purpose piece of threat-intelligence enrichment, built to run continuously going forward -- it isn't wired to any specific incident, and nothing in this lesson claims it will catch every kind of compromise. It checks sign-in IPs against one outside reputation feed, once a day, and surfaces what that feed already knows.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Confirm the KQL pull against real sign-in data

```kql
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where isnotempty(IPAddress)
| summarize SignInCount = count(), Users = make_set(UserPrincipalName, 10)
    by IPAddress
```

```
PRIYA:    That's pulling somewhere between 80 and 150 distinct IPs a
          day across the tenant -- branch offices, VPN egress, remote
          staff, and whatever automation is signing in too. Checking
          all of those against AbuseIPDB by hand every day isn't
          realistic, which is exactly why this needs to be a script.
```

## Step 2 -- Write the full script

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
ip-reputation-enrichment.py
Oakmere Credit Union -- Security Engineering
Scheduled Azure Automation Runbook (Python 3, daily @ 02:00 UTC)

Pulls distinct source IP addresses from the last 24 hours of
Entra sign-in logs in law-oakmere-soc, checks each one against
AbuseIPDB's IP reputation API, and writes any IP scoring above the
malicious threshold into a custom Sentinel log table
(IPReputationEnrichment_CL) for SOC triage.
"""
import os
import time
from datetime import datetime, timezone

import requests
from azure.identity import ManagedIdentityCredential
from azure.monitor.query import LogsQueryClient
from azure.monitor.ingestion import LogsIngestionClient

WORKSPACE_ID = os.environ["LAW_OAKMERE_SOC_WORKSPACE_ID"]
DCE_ENDPOINT = os.environ["OAKMERE_DCE_ENDPOINT"]
DCR_IMMUTABLE_ID = os.environ["IP_REPUTATION_DCR_ID"]
STREAM_NAME = "Custom-IPReputationEnrichment_CL"
ABUSEIPDB_KEY = os.environ["ABUSEIPDB_API_KEY"]
MALICIOUS_SCORE_THRESHOLD = 75  # AbuseIPDB confidence score, 0-100

credential = ManagedIdentityCredential()
logs_client = LogsQueryClient(credential)
ingestion_client = LogsIngestionClient(endpoint=DCE_ENDPOINT, credential=credential)

KQL_DISTINCT_SIGNIN_IPS = """
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where isnotempty(IPAddress)
| summarize SignInCount = count(), Users = make_set(UserPrincipalName, 10)
    by IPAddress
"""


def get_signin_ips():
    response = logs_client.query_workspace(
        workspace_id=WORKSPACE_ID,
        query=KQL_DISTINCT_SIGNIN_IPS,
        timespan=None,
    )
    table = response.tables[0]
    return [
        {"ip": row[0], "signInCount": row[1], "users": row[2]}
        for row in table.rows
    ]


def check_ip_reputation(ip_address):
    resp = requests.get(
        "https://api.abuseipdb.com/api/v2/check",
        headers={"Key": ABUSEIPDB_KEY, "Accept": "application/json"},
        params={"ipAddress": ip_address, "maxAgeInDays": 90},
        timeout=10,
    )
    resp.raise_for_status()
    data = resp.json()["data"]
    return {
        "abuseConfidenceScore": data["abuseConfidenceScore"],
        "countryCode": data.get("countryCode"),
        "isTor": data.get("isTor", False),
        "totalReports": data.get("totalReports", 0),
    }


def main():
    flagged_records = []
    for entry in get_signin_ips():
        try:
            reputation = check_ip_reputation(entry["ip"])
        except requests.RequestException as exc:
            print(f"WARN: reputation lookup failed for {entry['ip']}: {exc}")
            continue

        if reputation["abuseConfidenceScore"] >= MALICIOUS_SCORE_THRESHOLD:
            flagged_records.append({
                "TimeGenerated": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
                "IPAddress": entry["ip"],
                "SignInCount": entry["signInCount"],
                "AffectedUsers": entry["users"],
                "AbuseConfidenceScore": reputation["abuseConfidenceScore"],
                "CountryCode": reputation["countryCode"],
                "IsTor": reputation["isTor"],
                "TotalReports": reputation["totalReports"],
            })
        time.sleep(1.2)  # stay under AbuseIPDB's free-tier rate limit

    if flagged_records:
        ingestion_client.upload(
            rule_id=DCR_IMMUTABLE_ID,
            stream_name=STREAM_NAME,
            logs=flagged_records,
        )
        print(f"Flagged {len(flagged_records)} malicious IP(s) into {STREAM_NAME}.")
    else:
        print("No sign-in IPs crossed the malicious threshold today.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

```

## Step 3 -- Provision the Data Collection Rule and custom table

```bash
az monitor data-collection-endpoint create \
  --name dce-oakmere-soc \
  --resource-group rg-oakmere-soc \
  --location eastus

az monitor data-collection-rule create \
```

lessons.title: Rolling Out Zero-Trust Micro-Segmentation for svc-core-banking-sync
lessons.summary: Locking svc-core-banking-sync's network reach down to only the one database and vendor endpoint it actually needs -- the one control, built weeks before anyone knows it matters, that keeps a phished service account from going anywhere once it's inside.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Up to now, `svc-core-banking-sync` -- the service account behind the nightly core-banking sync job -- has lived on `vm-core-banking-sync`, inside `snet-core-banking-sync` on Oakmere Credit Union's production network, `vnet-oakmere-prod`. Like most internal subnets on a flat corporate network, it can currently reach almost anything else in `10.20.0.0/16`: the HR database, the member-services reporting warehouse, domain controllers, all of it. Nobody designed that access on purpose. It's just what a flat network gives you by default.

This lesson closes that gap. Renata Ibarra and the infrastructure team build a dedicated Network Security Group, `nsg-core-banking-sync`, and attach it to the subnet that one VM lives in. The NSG does one thing: it denies everything by default, and explicitly allows only the two destinations `svc-core-banking-sync` actually needs -- the private endpoint for `sql-oakmere-core-banking`, the specific database it syncs, and the documented static egress range for Vantage Core Systems, the third-party vendor whose core-banking platform it talks to. Everything else this account's traffic used to be able to reach is now a deny, logged by NSG flow logs feeding into Sentinel.

This is the least glamorous lesson in the whole series, and it is also the one that ends up mattering the most. Nobody building this NSG today knows that in a few lessons, this exact account gets phished. What this lesson buys, before anyone needs it, is a hard ceiling on how far that compromise can ever travel.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a credit union keeps one employee whose only job, every night, is to carry a folder of numbers between two specific filing cabinets -- cabinet A and cabinet B -- down one specific hallway. Right now, that employee has a master key that happens to open every door in the whole building, even though they never use any door but the one between cabinet A and cabinet B.

This lesson takes that master key away and gives the employee a key that only opens those two doors. Nothing else changes about their job -- the folder still gets carried every night, right on schedule. But if someone ever stole that employee's badge and pretended to be them, that stolen badge still wouldn't open the door to the vault, or the HR office, or anywhere else in the building. It would only open the two doors it was ever supposed to open. That's the entire point of this lesson: shrinking what one account can reach, before anyone needs that shrinking to matter.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Micro-segmentation is the practical, enforceable half of "assume breach": if you genuinely accept that a credential will eventually be compromised, the only lever left that still limits the damage is how much that credential can reach once it's in someone else's hands. `svc-core-banking-sync` is an unusually good candidate for this because its legitimate traffic pattern is exactly two destinations, every night, on a predictable schedule -- a database private endpoint and one vendor's documented egress range. That narrowness is what makes a tight, explicit-allow NSG actually practical here, rather than a compliance exercise that quietly gets a wildcard rule bolted on six months later because something broke.

The implementation detail worth being precise about is the default-deny baseline. `nsg-core-banking-sync` is built with two narrow allow rules at low priority numbers and an explicit deny-all-outbound rule at priority 4096 -- not relying on Azure's own implicit deny, because an explicit, logged deny rule is what actually shows up in NSG flow logs as a denied attempt, which is the signal this lesson's validation test depends on. Flow logs from this NSG are wired into the Sentinel workspace, `law-oakmere-soc`, which means every future attempt by this account's traffic to reach anything outside its two allowed destinations becomes a queryable, alertable event, not a silent drop. That logging pipeline is what turns a network control into a detection control -- it's not enough that the attacker can't get anywhere; the team also needs to be able to see that they tried.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Confirm the current, overly broad reach

Before building the NSG, Renata and the infra team confirm exactly how much `vm-core-banking-sync` can currently reach, so the before/after is documented rather than assumed:

```
CURRENT STATE -- snet-core-banking-sync (10.20.4.0/27)
  No NSG attached. Subnet inherits vnet-oakmere-prod's default
  routing -- effectively any-to-any within 10.20.0.0/16.

  Confirmed reachable today (manual test from vm-core-banking-sync):
    10.20.2.0/24   HR database subnet         REACHABLE (should not be)
    10.20.6.0/24   Member-reporting warehouse  REACHABLE (should not be)
    10.20.4.15/32  sql-oakmere-core-banking    REACHABLE (needed)
    203.0.113.40/29  Vantage Core Systems       REACHABLE (needed)
```

## Step 2 -- Build the NSG with an explicit default-deny

```bash
az network nsg create \
  --resource-group rg-oakmere-core-banking \
  --name nsg-core-banking-sync \
  --location eastus2

# Allow: the one database this job syncs to, over its private endpoint
az network nsg rule create \
  --resource-group rg-oakmere-core-banking \
  --nsg-name nsg-core-banking-sync \
  --name Allow-CoreBankingSyncDB \
  --priority 100 \
  --direction Outbound \
  --access Allow \
  --protocol Tcp \
  --destination-address-prefixes 10.20.4.15/32 \
  --destination-port-ranges 1433

# Allow: Vantage Core Systems' documented, static vendor egress range
az network nsg rule create \
  --resource-group rg-oakmere-core-banking \
  --nsg-name nsg-core-banking-sync \
  --name Allow-VantageCoreVendorGateway \
  --priority 110 \
  --direction Outbound \
  --access Allow \
  --protocol Tcp \
  --destination-address-prefixes 203.0.113.40/29 \
  --destination-port-ranges 443

# Deny everything else, explicitly, logged, last
az network nsg rule create \
  --resource-group rg-oakmere-core-banking \
  --nsg-name nsg-core-banking-sync \
  --name Deny-AllOtherOutbound \
  --priority 4096 \
  --direction Outbound \
  --access Deny \
  --protocol '*' \
  --destination-address-prefixes '*' \
  --destination-port-ranges '*'
```

## Step 3 -- Attach the NSG and turn on flow logs into Sentinel

```bash
az network vnet subnet update \
  --resource-group rg-oakmere-core-banking \
  --vnet-name vnet-oakmere-prod \
  --name snet-core-banking-sync \
  --network-security-group nsg-core-banking-sync

az network watcher flow-log create \
  --resource-group rg-oakmere-core-banking \
  --location eastus2 \
  --name fl-core-banking-sync \
  --nsg nsg-core-banking-sync \
  --storage-account stoakmeresoclogs \
  --workspace law-oakmere-soc \
  --enabled true \
  --retention 90
```

## Step 4 -- Validate the sync job still works

```
VALIDATION -- nightly core-banking sync (first run post-NSG)
  Scheduled run: 02:00 UTC
  sql-oakmere-core-banking write:     SUCCESS, 0 errors
  Vantage Core Systems API call:      SUCCESS, 200 OK
  Rows synced:                        14,882 (matches prior-night baseline)
```

## Step 5 -- Validate the lockdown by trying to go somewhere it shouldn't

```bash
# From vm-core-banking-sync, attempt the HR subnet it used to reach freely
Test-NetConnection -ComputerName 10.20.2.10 -Port 1433
# Result: TcpTestSucceeded : False
```

```kql
// law-oakmere-soc -- confirm the attempt was denied AND logged
AzureNetworkAnalytics_CL
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where NSGList_s has "nsg-core-banking-sync"
| where FlowStatus_s == "D"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIP_s, DestIP_s, DestPort_d, FlowStatus_s
```

```
TimeGenerated          SrcIP_s        DestIP_s      DestPort_d  FlowStatus_s
2026-09-xx 14:02:11    10.20.4.8      10.20.2.10    1433        D
```

The attempt is denied, and it's a queryable event in Sentinel -- not a silent drop. `svc-core-banking-sync` can now reach exactly two things, and nothing else is reachable even if someone is holding its credentials.

Attached to snet-core-banking-sync, flow logs enabled into law-oakmere-soc. Validated the nightly sync job still runs clean and that a test connection to an unrelated internal subnet is denied and logged.

The nightly job itself is unaffected; we confirmed it ran clean the same night.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've tightened the network access for one of our most sensitive automated jobs -- the one that moves core banking data every night -- so it can only reach the two systems it's actually supposed to talk to. If that account's credentials were ever stolen, this change on its own would stop an attacker from reaching anything else on our network.

lessons.title: A DevSecOps Pipeline Pass: Secrets Scanning and IaC Scanning
lessons.summary: Adding a secrets-scanning and infrastructure-as-code-scanning gate to the pipeline that ships Oakmere's own security infrastructure -- catching a near-repeat of the exact over-broad-access mistake Lesson 13 just fixed, before it ever reaches production this time.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Every control Oakmere's security team has built so far -- the Conditional Access policies, the Sentinel analytics rules, last lesson's NSG -- lives as Bicep and GitHub Actions in the team's own `oakmere/soc-infrastructure` repository. That repository has had no automated security gate of its own. A secret could get hardcoded into a template and merged. A badly scoped NSG rule could ship with a wildcard nobody caught in review. Nothing in the pipeline was watching for either.

This lesson closes that gap with two new pipeline jobs. A secrets-scanning job runs Gitleaks against every pull request, blocking the merge if it finds a credential, connection string, or API key committed in plaintext -- including, this run, the threat-intel API key `ip-reputation-enrichment.py` uses, caught in a draft commit before it ever reached `main`. An infrastructure-as-code scanning job runs Microsoft Security DevOps' Checkov integration against every Bicep template, blocking the merge on high-severity misconfigurations -- and on this very first run, it catches a draft template for a new reporting VM whose NSG rule uses a wildcard destination, almost exactly the kind of over-broad access Lesson 13 just spent a whole lesson removing. This time, a scanner catches it in a pull request, not an incident six months later.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a school finally hires a security guard for its building -- but doesn't give that guard a metal detector or a way to check what's in people's bags. People could walk in with anything and nobody would know until something went wrong.

This lesson gives the guard two actual tools. The first checks every box of parts coming into the building for anything dangerous left inside by mistake, like a key to the vault accidentally taped to a delivery box -- if it finds one, the box doesn't get through. The second checks every blueprint for a new room before it gets built, making sure nobody accidentally designs a door that opens onto a hallway it was never supposed to reach. On the very first day these two tools are turned on, the second one catches exactly that kind of mistake in a blueprint for a brand-new room -- the same kind of too-many-doors mistake the team had just spent real effort fixing somewhere else in the building, caught this time before a single wall was built.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A security team's own infrastructure repository is an unusually high-value target for exactly the kind of mistake this lesson guards against, precisely because the people committing to it are moving fast and trust each other -- which is exactly when a hardcoded secret or an overly permissive rule slips past code review unnoticed. Gating the pipeline itself closes that gap without depending on any individual reviewer catching it every time.

The secrets-scanning job runs Gitleaks against the full diff of every pull request, not just the files changed, which matters because a secret can be introduced in one commit and appear removed in a later one while still sitting in the repository's history. A verified-regex match -- a connection string pattern, a recognizable API key format -- fails the job and blocks merge, the same way a failing unit test would; it does not merely warn. The infrastructure-as-code scan runs the Microsoft Security DevOps CLI's Checkov integration against every Bicep template in the PR, checking for the category of misconfiguration this team now has direct, recent experience with: overly broad network rules, missing default-deny baselines, resources exposed without a private endpoint. Severity is the threshold that decides whether the gate blocks or merely annotates -- high and critical findings block the merge; medium and low findings surface as PR comments for the team to triage, a decision made explicitly rather than defaulted, because an overly strict gate on low-severity noise is exactly the kind of friction that gets a team routing around the scanner instead of fixing root causes. That the very first real run of this gate catches a wildcard NSG rule on a draft template -- the same category of mistake Lesson 13's work was built to correct elsewhere on the network -- isn't a coincidence worth downplaying; it's the clearest possible argument for why this gate belongs in the pipeline permanently rather than as a one-time cleanup.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Add the secrets-scanning job

```yaml
# .github/workflows/soc-infra-ci.yml
name: soc-infrastructure-ci
on: [pull_request]

jobs:
  secrets-scan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - name: Gitleaks scan
        uses: gitleaks/gitleaks-action@v2
        env:
          GITLEAKS_ENABLE_COMMENTS: true
        # fails the job (and blocks merge) on any verified match
```

## Step 2 -- The scan catches a real leaked key on its first run

```
GITLEAKS SCAN -- PR #142 (ip-reputation-enrichment.py config update)
  Finding:   generic-api-key
  File:      runbooks/ip-reputation-enrichment/config.bicep, line 18
  Match:     threatIntelApiKey = 'tk_live_7f3a9c...' (redacted)
  Severity:  CRITICAL -- live credential committed in plaintext
  Result:    PR BLOCKED. Author rotates the key, moves it to Key
             Vault, references it via @Microsoft.KeyVault(...) instead.
```

## Step 3 -- Add the infrastructure-as-code scanning job

```yaml
  iac-scan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Microsoft Security DevOps (Checkov)
        uses: microsoft/security-devops-action@v1
        id: msdo
        with:
          categories: 'IaC'
      - name: Fail on high/critical findings
        run: |
          if grep -qE 'HIGH|CRITICAL' ${{ steps.msdo.outputs.sarifFile }}; then
            echo "High/critical IaC findings present -- blocking merge."
            exit 1
          fi
```

## Step 4 -- The scan catches a near-repeat of Lesson 13's mistake

```
CHECKOV SCAN -- PR #145 (new reporting VM, draft Bicep template)
  Check:     CKV_AZURE_9 -- NSG rule should not permit unrestricted
             destination (*)
  Resource:  Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups/nsg-rpt-vm-draft
  Rule:      Allow-Outbound, destinationAddressPrefix: '*'
  Severity:  HIGH
  Result:    PR BLOCKED. Author scopes the rule to the two specific
             destinations the reporting VM actually needs, the same
             pattern used for nsg-core-banking-sync in Lesson 13.
```

## Step 5 -- Set the triage policy for lower-severity findings

```
SEVERITY POLICY -- soc-infrastructure-ci
  CRITICAL / HIGH  -> blocks merge, must be fixed or explicitly
                      waived in writing by the security lead
  MEDIUM / LOW     -> posted as a PR comment, tracked, does not
                      block merge -- avoids pipeline friction that
                      would push the team to route around the gate
```

## Step 6 -- Confirm both gates are required checks on `main`

```bash
gh api repos/oakmere/soc-infrastructure/branches/main/protection \
  --method PUT \
  --field required_status_checks[strict]=true \
  --field 'required_status_checks[contexts][]=secrets-scan' \
  --field 'required_status_checks[contexts][]=iac-scan'
```

Both jobs are now required checks -- a pull request to `oakmere/soc-infrastructure` cannot merge to `main` with an unresolved critical secret or a high/critical IaC finding, full stop.

First real run caught a live threat-intel API key committed in plaintext (PR #142) and a wildcard-destination NSG rule on a draft reporting-VM template (PR #145) -- the same over-broad-access pattern Lesson 13 just remediated elsewhere. Both blocked before merge. Severity policy: high/critical blocks, medium/low surfaces as a tracked PR comment.

Both caught real issues on their very first run, including almost repeating a network-access mistake we'd just fixed elsewhere -- caught this time before it went anywhere near production.

Those safeguards already caught two real issues on their first day running.

lessons.title: 36 Hours Late: Tracing the Sign-In Nobody Caught
lessons.summary: A phished service account signs in from a country Oakmere has no business in, and Sentinel stays silent -- until Renata's threat-intel automation flags the IP a day and a half later, and she traces it back to a dual exclusion nobody had connected until now.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Credentials for `svc-core-banking-sync` are phished through a compromised support portal belonging to Vantage Core Systems, the vendor whose core-banking platform the account syncs with nightly. On 2026-10-12 at 03:47 UTC, an attacker uses those credentials to sign into Entra ID tenant `oakmere-cu` -- interactively, from a hosting-provider IP geolocated to Romania, nowhere near Oakmere's Midwest footprint or Vantage's own documented egress range.

Nothing fires. `CA-RequireMFA-AllUsers` never challenges the sign-in, because `svc-core-banking-sync` sits in the exemption group `CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt`. And the Sentinel analytics rule "Impossible Travel - Interactive Sign-ins", built back in Lesson 9, never even evaluates the sign-in, because it excludes every account tagged `ServiceAccount` in Microsoft Entra's `IdentityInfo` table -- not just this account's non-interactive automation traffic, but this one, genuinely interactive, out-of-pattern sign-in too.

The first real signal doesn't come from Sentinel at all. It comes from `ip-reputation-enrichment.py`, the scheduled Azure Automation runbook Renata built in Lesson 12, which cross-references the previous day's sign-in IPs against a threat-intel feed every night at 02:00 UTC. The Romania IP isn't flagged maliciousas of the next night's run -- the threat-intel provider hadn't yet classified it. It's the run after that, at 2026-10-14 02:00 UTC -- roughly 36 hours after the sign-in -- that the feed catches up and the IP comes back flagged. This lesson is Renata picking up that flag the next morning and tracing it, step by step, back to the exact rule that should have caught this on day one and didn't.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a bank has a rule: any employee badge used in a city the bank doesn't operate in should set off an alarm right away. But there's also a second rule that says the night-shift cleaning crew's badges never set off that alarm, because they sometimes badge in from odd places doing legitimate work. One cleaner's badge gets cloned, and the thief uses it to badge into the building from a city the real cleaner has never been to -- and because of that second rule, the alarm that was supposed to catch exactly this never even looks at it.

Nobody finds out from the alarm system. A separate nightly check -- a list the bank keeps of "known bad" cities and devices, updated by an outside service -- doesn't have that city flagged as suspicious yet the next day. It's not until the day after that the outside service catches up and adds it to the bad list. That's when someone at the bank finally notices, a full day and a half after the badge was used, and has to go back through the records asking: how did this happen, and why didn't the alarm that was supposed to catch it ever go off?
lessons.explainProfessional:
The investigation's real value is in showing that the alert's silence was structural, not a tuning miss -- it would have stayed silent at any volume, on any day, because the exclusion logic never evaluated the sign-in's actual characteristics at all. Renata's first move, once the threat-intel flag surfaces, is to pull the raw sign-in record directly from `SigninLogs` rather than trusting any dashboard's summary of it -- the same instinct this series has taught repeatedly: go to the primary data, not the layer built on top of it.

What that record shows is a sign-in with every property that should have triggered scrutiny: `ResultType == 0` (succeeded), `IsInteractive == true`, a location with no prior history for this account, and `ConditionalAccessStatus` showing the CA policy was evaluated and explicitly not applied, because of the exemption group membership. From there, Renata reconstructs the Lesson 9 rule's actual exclusion logic and runs it by hand against this exact account, which is the step that converts a hunch into a confirmed root cause: the rule builds its exclusion list from `IdentityInfo` tags, and `svc-core-banking-sync` carries the `ServiceAccount` tag for an entirely unrelated, legitimate reason -- so it is removed from the Impossible Travel rule's candidate pool before the rule ever asks whether a given sign-in was interactive, automated, or anything else. The tag-based exclusion doesn't distinguish this account's real nightly non-interactive sync traffic from a rare, genuinely interactive sign-in using the same identity -- it excludes all of it, indiscriminately, which is precisely the condition an attacker holding this account's credentials walked straight into. The lesson closes with the mechanism fully understood and documented, and with one piece of good news confirmed before anything else happens: a check of NSG flow logs from Lesson 13's segmentation work shows zero denied or otherwise anomalous outbound attempts from `vm-core-banking-sync` during or after the compromise window -- the attacker authenticated, but never moved anywhere this account wasn't already allowed to go.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- The compromise, invisible in real time

```
2026-10-12  03:47 UTC
  Vantage Core Systems support portal (third-party vendor) is
  compromised. svc-core-banking-sync's credentials, reused on that
  portal, are harvested.

2026-10-12  03:52 UTC
  Interactive sign-in to oakmere-cu using svc-core-banking-sync's
  credentials, from IP 185.220.xx.xx (hosting provider, Romania).
  CA-RequireMFA-AllUsers: not applied (CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt)
  Sentinel "Impossible Travel - Interactive Sign-ins": did not evaluate
  Result: sign-in succeeds. No alert. No page. Nothing.
```

## Step 2 -- The only signal: a nightly automation, a day and a half late

```

  185.220.xx.xx checked against threat-intel feed: NOT yet flagged

2026-10-14  02:00 UTC  ip-reputation-enrichment.py run
  185.220.xx.xx checked against threat-intel feed: FLAGGED (malicious,
  known hosting-provider range associated with credential abuse)
```

lessons.title: Containment, Eradication, and the Corrected Rule
lessons.summary: Confirming the blast radius held, retiring svc-core-banking-sync's MFA exemption for certificate-based auth, shipping the corrected Impossible Travel rule scoped by sign-in type instead of account tag, and proving it with a test sign-in that finally fires.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Diagnosis in hand, this lesson is where Renata and the SOC team actually close the incident out -- containment, eradication, and a fix that holds for every account like this one going forward, not just this one.

Containment is mostly already done: Lesson 13's NSG confirmed zero lateral movement, so the immediate step is disabling the compromised credential and confirming no other sessions or tokens are still live. Eradication retires the root enabler on the identity side: `svc-core-banking-sync` comes out of `CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt` entirely, and its nightly sync to Vantage Core Systems is re-authenticated using a certificate bound to the Azure Automation runbook's managed identity -- meaning the account no longer performs a human-style, password-based sign-in at all, so there's nothing left for a phished credential to compromise in the first place.

The centerpiece is the corrected Sentinel rule. The new "Impossible Travel - Interactive Sign-ins" query drops the account-tag exclusion entirely and replaces it with a narrow, sign-in-type-based one: it excludes a sign-in only when it is genuinely non-interactive *and* comes from the automation account's own known application ID -- never by account identity alone. Renata proves the fix the same way she'd prove any fix in this series: by testing it. A controlled test sign-in, flagged interactive, using `svc-core-banking-sync`'s identity, is run against the corrected rule -- and this time, it fires.
lessons.explainSimple:
Remember the bank whose alarm rule exempted the whole night cleaning crew, badge and all, so a cloned badge used from the wrong city never set off any alarm? This lesson is the bank fixing that properly, in four parts.

First, they check the building cameras and confirm the thief never actually got past the front door they badged into -- the badge only ever opened that one entrance, nothing else, so there's nothing else to clean up.

Second, they take that cleaner's badge away entirely and replace it with something a thief can't clone the same way -- a special key that's physically tied to one specific door and can't be copied like a badge number can.

Third, and most important, they rewrite the alarm rule itself. Instead of saying "never alarm on anyone from the cleaning crew," the new rule says "don't alarm on the cleaning crew's regular automated nightly delivery truck, specifically -- but anyone from that crew badging in by hand, in person, still sets off the alarm like anyone else would."

Fourth, they test it. They walk a test badge in, in person, pretending to be that same account, and this time the alarm actually goes off. That's the proof the fix works, not just a promise that it should.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Containment and eradication here are fast precisely because the harder structural work -- the network segmentation -- was already done two lessons ago; this lesson's real weight is in the identity-side eradication and the corrected detection logic, and in proving both rather than merely asserting them.

Eradication on the identity side is deliberately more than "rotate the password." Retiring `svc-core-banking-sync` from `CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt` and moving its authentication to a certificate bound to the Azure Automation managed identity removes the entire class of risk, not just this one instance of it -- a certificate bound to a specific managed identity has no password to phish, cannot be entered into a vendor portal by a human, and cannot produce the kind of interactive, human-style sign-in event that triggered this incident in the first place. This is the eradication step that actually matches the root cause, rather than one that only matches its symptom.

The corrected rule's actual change is narrow and precise, which is what makes it trustworthy: it stops asking "is this account one we've labeled a service account" and starts asking "is this specific sign-in event non-interactive, and does it come from this account's own known automation app registration." That reframing means a genuinely rare but real interactive sign-in from this identity -- exactly the shape the attacker's sign-in had -- is never excluded, no matter what tag sits on the account in `IdentityInfo`. Validating this with an actual test sign-in, rather than a code review of the query, matters because KQL logic that looks correct on inspection can still fail against a Sentinel analytics rule's actual scheduling, lookback window, or entity-mapping configuration -- the kind of gap that only shows up when the rule is actually exercised end to end, incident created and all.

```bash

az ad group member remove \
  --group CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt \
  --member-id <svc-core-banking-sync-object-id>

# Confirm only the other two legacy accounts remain -- not this one
az ad group member list --group CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt --query "[].displayName"
```

```
["svc-legacy-batch", "svc-legacy-reporting"]
```

```bicep

// -- no password, nothing a phishing page can capture
resource syncRunbook 'Microsoft.Automation/automationAccounts/runbooks@2023-11-01' = {
  name: 'core-banking-sync'
  parent: automationAccount
  identity: {
    type: 'SystemAssigned'
  }
  properties: {
    runbookType: 'PowerShell'

    // identity via a client certificate registered on the app, never a
    // username/password svc-core-banking-sync credential
  }
}
```

```
AUTH MIGRATION -- core-banking sync job
  Before:  svc-core-banking-sync, username + password, interactive-
           capable, exempted from MFA
  After:   System-assigned managed identity + client certificate,
           cannot be used interactively, cannot be "phished" the way
           a password can, no CA exemption needed or possible
```

## Part 3 -- Ship the corrected Sentinel rule

```kql
// "Impossible Travel - Interactive Sign-ins" -- CORRECTED
// Excludes ONLY true non-interactive sign-ins from this account's
// own known automation app registration. Never excludes by account
// tag or account identity alone.
let KnownAutomationAppIds = dynamic([
  "a1b2c3d4-5e6f-4a7b-8c9d-0e1f2a3b4c5d" // core-banking-sync runbook app registration
]);
SigninLogs
| where ResultType == 0
| where not(IsInteractive == false and AppId in (KnownAutomationAppIds))
| extend Country = tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion)
| summarize Countries = make_set(Country),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress),
            Timestamps = make_list(TimeGenerated)
       by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where array_length(Countries) > 1
```

```
WHAT CHANGED
  Old exclusion: UserPrincipalName !in (ServiceAccountUPNs)
                 -- sourced from the ServiceAccountTags watchlist;
                 drops the account entirely, by tag, always.
  New exclusion: not(IsInteractive == false and AppId in (KnownAutomationAppIds))
                 -- drops ONLY this account's genuine non-interactive
                 automation traffic. A real interactive sign-in from
                 this identity is never excluded, no matter what tag
                 sits on the account.
```

```
  Action: test interactive sign-in using svc-core-banking-sync's
          identity, from a non-Oakmere test IP, run with security

  Expected: corrected rule creates a Sentinel incident.

Sentinel incident created:
  Title: Impossible Travel - Interactive Sign-ins
  Entity: svc-core-banking-sync@oakmere-cu.onmicrosoft.com

  Status: Active -- routed to SOC on-call

Result: PASS. The exact sign-in shape from the 2026-10-12 incident
would now create an incident immediately, not 36 hours later.
```

```

Root cause: dual exclusion (CA group + account-tag-based analytics
rule exclusion) prevented any real-time detection of an interactive
sign-in from a phished service account credential.
Containment: confirmed complete, zero lateral movement (Lesson 13
segmentation held).
Eradication: account removed from CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt;
authentication re-platformed to managed identity + certificate,
eliminating the phishable credential entirely.
Detection fix: Impossible Travel rule corrected to exclude by sign-in
type and known AppId, never by account tag. Validated live with a
test sign-in that produced a Sentinel incident.
Status: CLOSED.
```
