lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine an inspector visits a credit union and writes down three real problems: the guards don't watch closely enough, nobody has a plan for what to do if someone breaks in, and a few side doors get to skip the metal detector because they're "just for deliveries." The credit union hires someone to fix all three. While she's building the new watching system, she even writes down, on purpose, ahead of time: "one of those delivery doors could someday let a real intruder through, and if that happens, our new alarm might miss it too, because we told the alarm to ignore that door." Everyone signs off on that written warning, because fixing it perfectly right then would take longer than the credit union could wait.

Months later, exactly that happens -- someone sneaks in through one of those doors with a stolen delivery badge. The new systems mostly worked: an inner set of locked doors kept the intruder boxed into one hallway the whole time. But the alarm did miss it, for about a day and a half, until a different check -- one that runs every night no matter what -- finally caught it. Now she has to go tell the three people who hired her: here's what we built, here's exactly what happened, and here's proof we'd already told you this exact thing could happen -- and look how fast we closed it once it did.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A leadership readout about a real security gap succeeds or fails on one decision: whether the presenter leads with the genuine capability that's now live, or lets the incident swallow the whole conversation. This lesson is built around the former, because both things are true, and Denise Okafor, Thomas Reyes, and Priya Nair need to hear both, in the right order, from the person who was in the room for every prior commitment this project made.

Lead with what's real: Sentinel and Defender XDR are watching \`oakmere-cu\` in workspace \`law-oakmere-soc\`, \`CA-RequireMFA-AllUsers\` enforces MFA tenant-wide with one named, risk-accepted, quarterly-reviewed exception group, zero-trust network segmentation is live, and \`ip-reputation-enrichment.py\` runs nightly as an independent second signal. Then name the incident by its exact mechanism, because precision is what earns trust here, not apology. \`svc-core-banking-sync\` was phished through credential reuse against the Vantage Core Systems vendor portal; the attacker signed in interactively from Romania on October 12; and two separately reasonable, separately documented decisions -- the account's MFA risk acceptance in \`CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt\`, and the Impossible Travel rule's tag-based exclusion built to kill automation noise -- combined to let that sign-in through without a single alert, for a full 36 hours, against a committed MTTD-1 target of 4 hours Denise herself signed off on.

The fact that makes this presentation credible rather than defensive is the one most incident reports never get to use: this exact scenario was named in writing during the targets-setting work, as an explicit stress test -- "a legacy service account, exempt from MFA and tagged to reduce alert noise, has a rare real sign-in from an unexpected country; do these targets actually hold for it?" -- and the answer, recorded honestly at the time, was that nobody yet knew. The finer-grained fix (exclude by sign-in type and application ID, not account tag) was even named explicitly during the detection-architecture design as the fix that would close that gap, and deliberately deferred as a documented V1 scoping decision rather than built immediately. That means this incident isn't a surprise failure of the program -- it's the realization of a risk the program had already identified, with a fix already designed and waiting, which is exactly why it could be shipped and validated before this meeting ever happened.

\`\`\`
OAKMERE CREDIT UNION -- WHAT'S ACTUALLY RUNNING TODAY

Tenant:         oakmere-cu
Detection:      Microsoft Sentinel (workspace law-oakmere-soc) + Defender XDR
Identity:       CA-RequireMFA-AllUsers enforcing MFA tenant-wide, with one

                default-deny) restricting lateral reach tenant-wide
Automation:     ip-reputation-enrichment.py -- independent, nightly,

Status:         Live, actively protecting production sign-in and network
                traffic across the credit union's identity estate
\`\`\`

## Step 3 -- Name the incident by its exact mechanism

\`\`\`
RENATA:  svc-core-banking-sync was phished through credential reuse
         against the Vantage Core Systems vendor portal. On October
         12th, the attacker signed in interactively from Romania.
         That sign-in should have been caught two different ways, and
         both of the reasons it wasn't are things we'd already written
         down. First: the account sits in CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-
         Exempt, a documented, risk-accepted MFA exception for accounts
         not yet migrated off password auth. Second: our Impossible
         Travel rule excludes any account tagged ServiceAccount
         entirely, by that tag alone, to kill noise from real automated
         multi-region sync traffic -- it never even asked whether this
         particular sign-in was interactive.
\`\`\`

\`\`\`
COMMITTED:  MTTD-1 -- 4 hours to detect a high-severity identity alert.
ACTUAL:     Approximately 36 hours -- caught only by ip-reputation-
            enrichment.py's next nightly run, not by the Sentinel rule
            built specifically for this pattern.
\`\`\`

Say this number out loud before anyone else has to ask for it.

## Step 5 -- State what was, and wasn't, exposed

\`\`\`
RENATA:  Flow logs confirm zero lateral movement for the full 36
         hours. The account's network reach was already limited by
         design to exactly two destinations -- the core-banking sync
         database and the Vantage Core Systems vendor connection --
         nothing else on the network was ever reachable. We found no
         evidence of data exfiltration beyond that already-narrow
         path.
\`\`\`

## Step 6 -- Make the credibility argument: this was a named, accepted risk

\`\`\`
ON THE RECORD, MONTHS BEFORE THIS HAPPENED:
"A legacy service account, exempt from MFA and tagged to reduce alert
noise, has a rare real interactive sign-in from an unexpected country.
Do MTTD-1 and COV-1 actually hold for THIS account?"
  -- flagged in writing during target-setting, signed off by Denise
     Okafor, reviewed by Thomas Reyes, owned going forward by Renata.

ALSO ON THE RECORD, DURING DETECTION DESIGN:
A finer-grained exclusion -- by sign-in type and application ID,
instead of account tag -- was explicitly named as the fix for exactly
this gap, and deliberately deferred as a documented V1 scoping
decision, reviewed and signed off at the time.
\`\`\`

This is the line that separates "we missed something" from "something we warned about happened, and we were ready." Say it plainly.

## Step 7 -- State the fix, and that it's already shipped

\`\`\`
FIX, ALREADY LIVE:
1. svc-core-banking-sync removed from CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt
   entirely; its nightly sync now runs on a certificate-bound managed
   identity that cannot be phished the same way.
2. The Impossible Travel rule's exclusion logic rewritten to exclude
   only genuine non-interactive sign-ins from this account's known
   automation app ID -- never by account tag alone again.
3. Validated with a controlled test sign-in reproducing the exact
   shape of the attacker's sign-in: a Sentinel incident now fires
   immediately, not 36 hours later.
STATUS: Incident closed.
\`\`\`

## Step 8 -- Rehearse the hard questions

\`\`\`
Q: If we already knew this was a risk, why wasn't it fixed sooner?
A: Because closing it required engineering time against a documented
   V1 scoping decision everyone signed off on, not an oversight. The
   incident is what reordered our priority list -- correctly.

Q: Could the same exclusion pattern exist on another rule right now?
A: Possibly. We've fixed this one rule and this one account. We have
   not yet audited every other Sentinel rule for the same tag-based
   pattern -- that's real, named, dated follow-up work, not something
   we're claiming is already done.
\`\`\`

## Step 9 -- Close by asking for explicit understanding, not reassurance

Ask Denise, Thomas, and Priya to confirm they understand two things clearly: why a tag-based exclusion could never have caught this sign-in regardless of severity, and that the corrected rule, the exemption removal, and the containment that held throughout are all already live and validated. lessons.explainProfessional:
A risk-register entry earns its place in a compliance file only if it's scored in the organization's own established language, because that's the language an examiner reads and the language that makes "we handled this correctly and quickly" a checkable claim rather than a assertion. This lesson scores the \`svc-core-banking-sync\` exclusion gap the same way Oakmere's GRC program scores every other finding -- and because the fix already shipped in the previous phase, the entry is written retrospectively, closing the loop rather than requesting it.

Scored honestly, the tag-based exclusion was a high-inherent-risk control gap: it silently disabled a specific detection rule for an entire class of accounts, with no compensating check on sign-in behavior, on exactly the class of account most attractive to a phishing attempt precisely because it's exempted from MFA. That risk was already named in writing during target-setting and detection-architecture planning -- this register entry is the first time it gets scored with real numbers instead of a hypothetical. The fix -- rescoping the exclusion to sign-in type and application ID, and retiring the matching CA exemption for this account -- drops the residual risk to low, because an interactive sign-in from an unfamiliar location on this account class is now evaluated by the rule rather than skipped outright, and the account no longer carries the exemption at all.

The cost side of the write-up is what makes the business case airtight rather than merely dutiful: the fix used tooling Oakmere already licensed and operated, cost roughly a sprint of a detection engineer's time, and required no new vendor, budget line, or headcount -- because the finer-grained approach had already been designed and signed off during architecture planning, waiting only for priority. The risk closed is a live instance of the exact finding category the credit union's regulatory exam had already cited, plus a quantified, already-realized cost of leaving it open: a 36-hour detection gap against a 4-hour committed target. Put side by side in the organization's own risk-register format, that comparison is the argument for why this got fixed in days, not quarters.

lessons.title: Writing the After-Action Report and Owning the Follow-Up
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
An incident that only lives in Renata's memory is a liability the moment she's out sick, on vacation, or has moved to a different team the next time something like this happens. This video writes the actual after-action report (AAR) for the \`svc-core-banking-sync\` incident: a precise, timestamped timeline from the Vantage Core Systems credential-reuse compromise through detection, containment confirmation, and the fix going live; a root cause stated as one honest sentence naming both exclusions; a clear accounting of what went right (zero-trust containment, the independent nightly automation) and what went wrong (the tag-based exclusion, and a real SLA miss against the committed 4-hour detection target); and four specific, owned, dated follow-up action items.

This is the document Oakmere's SOC hands to the next analyst, the next auditor, and the next regulatory examiner, so it has to hold up to all three readers at once: factual enough for an engineer, honest enough for an auditor, and complete enough that nobody has to reconstruct this incident from memory a year from now.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine after a school fire drill goes a little wrong -- the alarm didn't go off in one hallway because of a mix-up with the rules for that hallway -- the principal doesn't just say "that went fine, moving on." She writes down the exact time things happened, what the real mix-up was (without blaming any one teacher for it), what worked well (the fire doors that kept smoke from spreading), and a short list of exactly who is fixing what, and by when -- not "we'll be more careful," but "Ms. Reyes is checking every other hallway's rules by Friday, and Ms. Nair is updating the official safety file by the following week."

That's exactly what this video writes for the real computer-security version of that story: a clear timeline, an honest explanation of the real mix-up, what worked well, and a short list of exactly who is fixing what next, with real dates next to each name.
lessons.explainProfessional:
An AAR earns its place in the organization's memory only if every claim in it is specific enough to be checked by someone who wasn't in the room -- "the exclusion was too broad" is an impression; "the Impossible Travel rule's exclusion matched on the ServiceAccount tag alone, with no check on sign-in type or application ID, so it suppressed alerting for any sign-in from a tagged account regardless of how anomalous that sign-in was" is a fact a future engineer can verify against the rule definition itself.

The blameless framing matters most in the root-cause section, because the honest root cause here is a mismatch between two individually defensible, individually documented decisions -- a signed-off MFA risk acceptance for accounts mid-migration, and a detection rule's exclusion logic built to kill real automation noise -- not a mistake by any one engineer. Writing the root cause to name that mismatch precisely, and to note that the exact combination had already been flagged in writing as an open risk during target-setting, is what makes the document useful to the next person who builds an exclusion on a different rule, rather than a document that pretends this was unforeseeable.

The follow-up items need the specificity a real auditor or a future on-call engineer would demand: a named owner, a concrete action, and a real date, not "review exclusions periodically." A follow-up item without an owner is a wish; one without a date never gets prioritized against the next incident. This lesson writes all four with both, and ties them to processes that already exist -- like the quarterly CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt review -- rather than inventing new ones that compete with them.

## Step 1 -- Write the AAR header, blamelessly

\`\`\`
AFTER-ACTION REPORT -- SVC-CORE-BANKING-SYNC CREDENTIAL COMPROMISE
Tenant:     oakmere-cu
Workspace:  law-oakmere-soc
Severity:   High -- a core-banking integration service account was
            compromised for approximately 36 hours before detection
Target:     MTTD-1 (4 hours, high-severity identity alert) -- missed
Status:     Resolved. Credentials rotated, exemption removed, rule
            corrected and validated.
\`\`\`

## Step 2 -- Write the timeline factually, with real times

\`\`\`
2026-10-12, ~2:00 PM UTC  An attacker reuses credentials obtained from
                a compromise of the Vantage Core Systems vendor
                portal and authenticates as svc-core-banking-sync.
                The account signs in interactively from Romania.
2026-10-12, same moment   Two separately documented exclusions both
                let the sign-in through without alerting: the
                account's MFA risk acceptance in CA-Legacy-
                ServiceAccounts-Exempt, and the Impossible Travel
                rule's exclusion of any account tagged
                ServiceAccount, matched before the rule ever checks
                whether the sign-in was interactive.
2026-10-12 onward         Zero-trust network segmentation (nsg-core-
                banking-sync) confines the account's reachable
                network surface to exactly two destinations -- the
                core-banking sync database and the Vantage Core
                Systems vendor endpoint. No lateral movement occurs
                at any point.
2026-10-13, 02:00 UTC     ip-reputation-enrichment.py runs its normal
                nightly cycle (Automation Runbook
                aa-oakmere-security); the sign-in's source IP is
                not yet flagged on the threat-intel feed.
2026-10-14, 02:00 UTC     The same nightly run flags the source IP as
                malicious via AbuseIPDB and writes the hit to
                IPReputationEnrichment_CL. Elapsed time since the
                original sign-in: approximately 36 hours.
2026-10-14, shortly after Renata Ibarra pulls the raw sign-in record,
                confirms it was interactive, succeeded, and show
                Conditional Access as explicitly not applied --
                unlike the account's normal nightly automated
                traffic -- and opens a formal incident.
2026-10-14-15             Credentials rotated; root cause confirmed by
                reconstructing the Impossible Travel rule's logic by
                hand; containment confirmed via flow-log review;
                account removed from CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-
                Exempt and migrated to a certificate-bound managed
                identity; rule corrected to exclude by sign-in type
                and known application ID, not account tag; fix
                validated with a controlled test sign-in.
\`\`\`

## Step 3 -- State the root cause in one precise sentence

\`\`\`
ROOT CAUSE: Two individually documented decisions -- an MFA risk
acceptance for svc-core-banking-sync pending its migration off
password authentication, and a Sentinel exclusion built to suppress
alerting for any ServiceAccount-tagged identity regardless of sign-in
behavior -- combined so that neither Conditional Access nor the
Impossible Travel rule ever evaluated this sign-in on its actual
merits. This exact combination had been named in writing as an open
risk during target-setting, months before it occurred.
\`\`\`

## Step 4 -- State what went right and wrong, without embellishment

\`\`\`
WENT RIGHT:  Zero-trust network segmentation confined the attacker's
             reach to two destinations for the full 36 hours, with no
             evidence of lateral movement or data exfiltration beyond
             that already-narrow path. The independent nightly
             threat-intel automation caught the compromise on its own
             schedule, without needing a human to notice anything
             first.

WENT WRONG:  The one detection rule built specifically for this sign-
             in pattern was structurally unable to fire for this
             account, for the full 36 hours -- a direct miss against
             the 4-hour MTTD-1 target the team itself committed to.
\`\`\`

## Step 5 -- Write four follow-up items: owned, and dated

\`\`\`
1. Audit every other Sentinel analytics rule in law-oakmere-soc for the
   same tag-based (rather than behavior-based) exclusion pattern that
   let this sign-in through.
   Owner: Renata Ibarra.  Due: Wednesday, November 4, 2026.

2. Confirm every remaining member of CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt
   is on a tracked, dated migration plan to certificate-based or
   managed-identity authentication -- not left open-ended the way
   svc-core-banking-sync was before this incident.
   Owner: Thomas Reyes's identity team.  Due: Wednesday, November 11,
   2026.

3. Fold this incident explicitly into the next scheduled quarterly
   CA-Legacy-ServiceAccounts-Exempt review (already an existing,
   co-signed process) so the review checklist itself now asks whether
   any exclusion anywhere in the detection stack is still scoped by a
   static tag instead of actual sign-in behavior.
   Owner: Renata Ibarra and Thomas Reyes's identity team, jointly.
   Due: next scheduled quarterly review.

4. Update the regulatory exam response file with this finding's full,
   dated remediation record -- detection fix, exemption removal, and
   containment confirmation -- for the compliance record.
   Owner: Priya Nair, with Renata Ibarra.  Due: Friday, November 6,
   2026.
\`\`\`

## Step 6 -- Name ownership plainly, beyond the four items

\`\`\`
OWNERSHIP
  Detection engineering going forward:     Renata Ibarra (SOC Analyst)
  CA policy and exemption governance:      Thomas Reyes (Director, IT
                                           Infrastructure)
  Regulatory/exam liaison for this entry:  Priya Nair (Compliance &
                                           Risk Officer)
  Executive sponsor:                       Denise Okafor (VP,

\`\`\`

## Step 7 -- Store it where the next analyst will actually find it

Save this AAR in the SOC's shared incident log, link the four follow-up items to their tracked tickets, and walk Thomas Reyes through items 2 and 3 directly, since those are owned outside the SOC, and Priya Nair through item 4 directly, since the exam response file is hers to maintain.

lessons.title: Telling the Whole Story in a Job Interview: STAR, Start to Finish
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
This is the last video in the series, and it answers a question every one of these twenty lessons was quietly building toward: how does Renata Ibarra actually talk about this entire project in a job interview? Not the postmortem version, and not the risk-register version -- the version that has to work in ninety seconds, out loud, to an interviewer who has never heard of Oakmere Credit Union and is deciding, in real time, whether Renata can own a real security engineering problem end to end.

This video builds that answer as a complete, genuine STAR narrative -- Situation, Task, Action, Result -- that ties together every phase of this project: the regulatory exam's three findings that started it, the Sentinel detection, Conditional Access, and zero-trust work that followed, the real 36-hour detection gap that same work caught in itself, the already-scoped fix that closed it fast, and the documentation and follow-through that closed the loop. It is written to be used, not just admired -- a student reading this should be able to adapt it, almost sentence for sentence, into their own interview answer the next time they're asked "tell me about a security incident you handled."
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you spent months helping a credit union fix three real problems an inspector found, and partway through, the very alarm system you were building caught a real break-in that slipped past one of its own rules -- a rule you'd already written down, in advance, as a known weak spot. You were the one who found it, explained exactly why it happened, and fixed it so it can't happen the same way again. That's a genuinely great story. But in a job interview, you can't just say "it was a big project, it went fine" -- you have to tell it in a shape the interviewer can actually follow: what was the situation, what were you asked to do, what did you actually do, and what happened as a result.

This video writes that exact four-part version of the story for Renata, using the real details from this whole project -- not a made-up example, the actual one -- so it's ready to say out loud the next time someone asks her about it.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A STAR answer fails in interviews for one of two reasons almost every time: it's too vague to prove the candidate actually did the work ("we improved our monitoring"), or it's so deep in technical detail that the interviewer loses the thread before reaching the result. The version built here avoids both by anchoring every section in one specific, nameable fact from this project, while still compressing cleanly enough to deliver in under two minutes.

Situation: a regional credit union's regulatory examination returned three findings -- insufficient detection coverage, no documented incident-response process, and legacy service accounts bypassing MFA with no documented control. Task: as the SOC Analyst responsible for closing all three, Renata's job was to build real detection engineering in Microsoft Sentinel, harden Conditional Access with a documented, risk-accepted exception process, stand up zero-trust network segmentation, and build independent Python automation as a second line of defense -- all against detection and response targets she helped set and was held to. Action: during that build, she flagged in writing the exact stress scenario that would later happen -- a legacy, MFA-exempt, tag-excluded service account having a rare real interactive sign-in -- and her team made a documented, signed-off call to defer the finer-grained fix. Months later, a phished service account hit precisely that scenario; her own independent automation caught it about 36 hours later, missing their 4-hour detection target; she traced the exact mechanism, confirmed containment had held throughout, shipped and validated the fix her own team had already designed, and closed the loop with a blameless postmortem and four dated follow-up items. Result: the finding closed, zero data exposure confirmed, the detection gap fixed and tested, and the SLA miss became the evidence base for auditing every other rule in the system for the same pattern.

The interview-specific skill this lesson teaches is naming the result honestly rather than overselling it: the right closing line owns the gap as proof the system works, not as something to minimize or bury. An interviewer who hears a candidate say "we'd already flagged this exact risk in writing, and when it happened, our own tooling caught it and we closed it fast" trusts that candidate more than one who implies nothing ever goes wrong on their watch.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Set up the answer before diving into STAR

When an interviewer asks "tell me about a time you handled a security incident" or "walk me through a real project you've worked on end to end," resist starting mid-incident. Open with one sentence that frames the whole arc: "I'll walk you through a project that actually has two parts -- the security program I was hired to build, and a real incident that program caught in itself partway through, one we'd actually already flagged as a risk." That framing tells the interviewer this is a complete story, not just a crisis anecdote.

## Step 2 -- Situation: name the real starting point

\`\`\`
SITUATION (what Renata says):
"I was the SOC Analyst at a regional credit union. Our most recent
regulatory examination came back with three specific findings:
detection coverage was insufficient, we had no documented incident-
response process, and a handful of legacy service accounts were
bypassing MFA with no documented justification. All three had to be
remediated, and remediation was my responsibility."
\`\`\`

Keep this to two or three sentences. The interviewer needs the stakes and the three concrete findings, not the full exam report.

## Step 3 -- Task: state the concrete mandate

\`\`\`
TASK (what Renata says):
"My task had four parts: build real detection engineering in
Microsoft Sentinel so we'd actually catch anomalous sign-ins, harden
our Conditional Access policies so any MFA exception was named,
documented, and reviewed rather than silent, stand up zero-trust
network segmentation so a single compromised account couldn't reach
everything, and build independent automation as a second line of
defense. I also helped set, and was personally held to, specific
detection and response time targets."
\`\`\`

Four concrete deliverables plus a measurable commitment, no jargon the interviewer would have to stop and ask about.

## Step 4 -- Action: the part that actually proves the skill

\`\`\`
ACTION (what Renata says):
"While I was still designing the detection rules, I flagged something
in writing -- a specific stress scenario: what happens if one of our
MFA-exempt legacy service accounts, which we'd also tagged to cut
down on alert noise, ever had a real, malicious interactive sign-in?
We didn't yet know if our targets would hold for that case. We named a
more precise fix for it, and we made a documented, signed-off decision
to defer building it immediately, to ship the broader program first.

Months later, that exact scenario happened. One of our service
accounts was phished through a vendor's compromised portal, and it
signed in from a country it had never touched. It should have
triggered our new anomaly-detection rule, but it didn't, because of
the very gap we'd already named. It ran undetected for about 36 hours
-- well past the 4-hour target we'd committed to -- until my own
independent threat-intelligence automation caught it on its regular
nightly cycle.

I led the investigation. I traced the exact mechanism, confirmed our
network segmentation had already contained the account to a tiny,
fixed slice of the network the whole time, and then shipped the
finer-grained fix we'd already designed months earlier -- rescoping
the exclusion to actual sign-in behavior instead of a static tag, and
removing the account's MFA exemption entirely. I validated it with a
controlled test, then wrote the full blameless postmortem and a set of
dated, owned follow-up items, including auditing every other detection
rule for the same kind of gap."
\`\`\`

This is the longest section, and that's deliberate -- it's where the interviewer evaluates real technical ownership. Keep every sentence tied to something specific and checkable, never a general claim like "I improved our processes."

## Step 5 -- Result: state it honestly, and close on the reframe

\`\`\`
RESULT (what Renata says):
"The finding closed. We confirmed zero data exposure, because the
containment we'd built did exactly what it was designed to do. We
fixed the exact detection gap, validated it, and used the miss against
our own target as the reason to go audit every other rule in the
system for the same mistake before it could happen again anywhere
else.

The part I'm proudest of isn't that nothing went wrong. It's that we'd
already written down, in advance, that this exact thing could happen
-- and when it did, our own program caught it, contained it, and we
had the fix ready to ship. That's not a failure story. That's what a
security program working correctly actually looks like."
\`\`\`

## Step 6 -- Prepare for the two follow-up questions every interviewer asks

\`\`\`
Q: "Why did it take 36 hours instead of 4?"
A: "Because the one rule built for this exact pattern was structurally
   excluded from firing for this account -- a tradeoff we'd knowingly
   made and documented. The honest answer is our detection coverage
   had a real, named gap, and it was caught within one business cycle
   by a second, independent layer, before any real harm occurred."

Q: "What would you do differently if you were starting over?"
A: "I'd push harder to build the finer-grained version of an exclusion
   the first time, even under time pressure, rather than deferring it
   -- and I'd build the habit, now permanent on my team, of checking
   any new detection rule's exclusion logic against the exact
   condition it's meant to exempt, not a convenient proxy like a tag."
\`\`\`

## Step 7 -- Deliver it end to end, under two minutes

Practice the full S-T-A-R sequence out loud, timed. If it runs long, trim Situation and Task first -- Action and Result are where the real evidence of skill lives, and they should never be the part that gets cut for time.

## Series close

Twenty videos ago, this series opened with three regulatory exam findings at a credit union most people have never heard of. It closes here, with the exact same project turned into a two-minute answer a real candidate can use in a real interview -- because the whole point of building something end to end, honestly, including the part that was flagged as a risk and then actually happened, is that it's the only kind of story that survives being told out loud under pressure. Series complete.

Prepared Renata's responses to the two most likely follow-up questions: the detection-target miss and what she'd change building the same program again.

lessons.summary: The series finale: how Renata Ibarra tells this entire project as one STAR-format story in a job interview, from the regulatory exam through the fix.
